SANDERSVILLE. Ga, Feb. 10
One white boy and twenty-five
negro workmen were killed when a
tornado struck the mill village
Of the Cleveland-OcOnee Lumber
Company near here this afternoon.
About nifty dwellings, stores and
once buildings were blown down,
but the mill was only slightly dam,
aged. Ahsut thirty were injured,
eight or ten probably fatally. The
tornado also struck the village OF
Oconee, blowing down several
houses and injuring about ten peo-
Pile. none fatally. Neal Meier, pres
ident Of the lumber company, esu-
mated the damage at about $500
600.


The tornado came from the East
and Travelled along a narrow track
on the south side Of the Central
of Georgia Railroad. The mill
houses On that side Of the road
were demolished. The tornado
struck at noon when the employees
were at their homes.


The white boy killed, Bonnie Orr,
about II years old, was the son Of
a mill workman.

DUBLIN, April 2s.-Four Sim
Fein leaders, who were found guilty
by a British court martial of levying
war against British crown forces
from ambush, were executed in the
military barracks yard at Cork this
morning. They were executed In
couples. the first meeting death at s
o'clock; the second fifteen minutes
later.


Relatives and sympathizers knelt
in prayer outside the execution
ground while the death sentence was
being carried out.


The four men were Patrick O'Sul-
livan, Maurice Moore, Thomas Null
cahy, and Patrick Ronayne.


The municipal corporation council
and the Cork harbor board adopted
resolutions of protest against the
executions and announced that copies
had been sent to President Harding
a; Washington and Pope Benedict
Nv at Rome. The protest was based
upon the contention that the con-
demned men were not ordinary Grim
inals but prisoners of war.

NORFOLK. Va, Nov. 21.-Seventy-
five men and twelve officers, the crew
of the United States oiler Alameda.
were abliged to abandon that vessel
fifty miles off Cape Henry Saturday
night when the ship caught fire.


Wireless Tells Of Rescue.
Wireless messages from the burn.
ing ship and from the steamships
Palloa and Bristol advised Hampton
Roads Naval Base of the ships
plight and also that the crew had
been saved.


The Alameda was bound to Nor.
folk to load Christmas mail for
American soldiers and sailors over.
seas. She is a 10,000-tnn steel vessel.
Three naval tugs, including the Kel-
weden, and the Coast Guard cutter
Manning were rushed to the assist
ance of the Alameda.


Soon after fire was discovered the
crew made a heroic attempt to con-
quer 1t, but the flames spread rapidly
and the decks became too hot for
the men to work without danger of
having their feet blistered. There
was also danger that the ships big
fuel tank. filled with oil. would ex-
plode.


The crew took to the life boats and
were at the mercy of the high seas
for about four hours. Answering
the Alameda calls for assistance.
the steamers Bristol and Palloa
sighted the signal of distress and
displayed by the men in the life
boats and picked them up before
going to the assistance Of the burn.
ing craft.


Expect to Tow Ship In.
Naval officials said today the ship
probably would reach port In tow of
naval tugs.


Tons Of water were poured IN the
hold of the ship by naval tugs. The
Alameda is anchored about 46 miles
off Cape Henry.


Belief is expressed here that when
full details of the rescue are received.
q thrilling maritime story will be
narrated. Seamen say that with the
wind blowing as II has been. trip
on the sea in lifeboats must have
been a hazardous undertaking.

manship and seaworthiness, not

feet long and have displacements Of
$1,000 tons. When fully loaded they
draw thirty-three feet, and each has
accommodations for over 200 first
class passengers. Both liners develop
ed speeds Of over nineteen knots an
hour on their trial trips and shipping

selves, Joseph Orann, a mechanic who

Fitzgerald. snarling in liked grin

aim with his revolver and fired again

his heart and would have proved fatal.
At the second shot Orann took to
his heels, shouting: "Ill get cop."

through the doorway. He was back
within two minutes with Sergeant
kelleher and Patrolman Bauer, whom
he had found at Madison Avenue in
police side-car motorcycle.


Another pistol shot sounded as thev
turned into the garage and they found
Fitzgerald dead beside the man he had
killed. He had shot himself in the
head.


:. Finnerty was forty-two years old and
lived with him wife at 1850 Fifty
fourth Street, Brooklyn Fitzgerald
who was not married, was forty-five

because She sang 80 loud he could

dren. She began her singing lessons
when she was twelve years old. Her
voice was always natural and easy

technical things.


A real song recital she gave for the
first time when she was fifteen years
old. in Groningen and in Amsterdam.
She then became a pupil at the Am
sterdam Conservatory, where she
studied with Cornelie van Zanten.

to Berlin, and although she gave her
first recital there with great success.
she felt that she had so much to
learn she stopped giving concerts and
studied two years with Etelka Ger
ster. from whom she learned every
thing.

ATLANTIC CITY. June Jack
Dempsey ended his front-porch cam
paign to-day when he resumed training
after a four days lay-off by boxing six
rounds in his open-air arena with three
heavyweight sparring partners.


Between 600 and TOO spectators filed
into the arena TO watch the workout
after paying dollar admission, in
stead of fifty cents, the price charged
for the first two weeks of the cham
pion's training.


Jack Kearns, Dempsey's manager,
said admission of 81 would be charged
CT. Saturday and Sunday and, perhaps,
or week days for the final two weeks

increased admission this afternoon

AS result of his layoff Dempsey
was in condition to set a fast pace, but
he did not open Up until Larry Will
llams faced him for the final two
rounds of boxing. Martin Burke, the

Renault, and a clever boxer. He forced

ropes for the third and fourth rounds.


Dempsey employed his famous shift
against Renault and Williams, feinting
them into left-hand leads and then
hooking them with solid left hooks to
the body and head. Dempsey also dis
played his cleverness in straight right
hand hitting. When Williams and
Renault led with a left, Dempsey
whipped over his right on the inside
instead of hooking it on the outside.
Once Dempsey caught Williams flush

him up for few seconds until Will

DUBLIN, March 14.-Six Irishmen
paid the extreme penalty for fight
ing for Irish freedom at Mountjoy
prison at daybreak this morning.
During the executions 10000 men.
women and children chanted the Of
fees for the dead, outside the pris-
on walls.


They died like the heroes they
WERE" said Canon Walters. the
Roman Catholic priest who, admin
istered the last sacraments to the
~ Affairs Erected.


The scene about Mountjoy prison
was the imost impressive witnessed
in Dublin in many years. The kneel-
ing mourners in the roadways re-
sembled a huge religious service.
Rude affairs erected just outside the
prison walls were surmounted by
burning candles. while priests min
gled with the throng leading in the
singing of hymns and the reciting
Of rosaries.


There was no dry eye in the great
multitude and a great cry of an
guish went up as the nearby church
bells tolled the fatal hours-six,
seven, eight.


Canon Walters was the only man
present who discussed the last
scenes. He declared that the men
were unmoved and their eyes were
bright, and that they were glad to
die in the cause of Irish freedom.
Not one OF them finched, he said,
when the black caps were placed
upon their heads and all walked to
the eallows with firm step.


Work Suspended.


There was a total stoppage of
work in Dublin until after IL
o'clock. Even the postofice and
the government employees and
schools Joined in the universal
mark of sympathy.


Premier Lloyd Georges refusal to
be moved by appeals for reprieye
which came from all parts of Eng
land and ireland over the weekend
stirred the popular emotions to such
an extent that extensive reprisals
on the part of the Sim Feiners are
feared by the military authorities.
Immediately after the executions
Dublin Castle ordered all soldiers
confined to their barracks for an
indefinite period.


Guards on Duty.


During the hours that the mul-
titudes were watching at the gates
of the prison, armored cars full of
soldiers guarded the prison walls
and an aeroplane droned overhead
from sunrise on.


The men who were executed were
Patrick Moran. Thomas wheian,
Frank Flood, Bernard Ryan, Thomas
Bryan and Patrick Doyle. All
were accused of participation in
ambushes which resulted in the
deaths of members of the British
Intelligence ONCE.


When the warders of the prison
posted the notices that the execu-
tions had been carried out the
crowds outside the walls maintained
absolute silence for several min
utes.


Wife Collapses.


The wife of Patrick Doyle two
weeks ago gave birth to twin sons.
One of the babies died and was
buried today. She was not told of
her husbands doom until Saturday,
and she visited with the surviving
twin on Sunday to bid him goodby.
Today she collapsed.

ROME, May S.~-The battles between
the Fascist, or Extreme 'Nationalists,
and the Communists in various parts
of Italy are becoming even more bitter
as the elections draw nearer. On
Friday alone the reports of wide
spread violence showed total of six
dead and forty wounded. The con-
fiicts of that day included one at Cit
tadella, near Padua, in which the Fas-
cisti in avenging Communist assault,
attempted to destroy the labor head
quarters. All the, attacking party, how
ever, were arrested and imprisoned


When news of the wholesale i'm
prisonment reached the Fascist head
quarters in Padua several hundred
members of the organization, sent out
for the purpose of liberating their
comrades, went to Cittadella, forced
one of the prisons in which part of
the arrested men had been placed, and
overcame the carabineer guards there.
Fascist Besiege Prison
Flushed with their success, the Fas-
cisti proceeded to the other prison,
where the guards refused them en-
trance. Shots were fred and the guard
officer ordered the Fascist away. The
latter, however, insisted upon the
liberation Of the prisoners, and an
other volley was fired, the officer fall
ing wounded.


Upon this the carabineers opened fire
and a fusiliade occurred, in which sew
eral combatants were Wounded. The
carabineers inside the walls fired first
in the air and then into the crowd
The Fascist again tried to storm the
place, but failed, their attacks alto
gether resulting in three of their num-
Der being killed and ten others being
wounded.


Commerce Chamber Bombed


A dispatch to the Epoca from
Florence reports the chamber of labor
at Rifridi being set on fire with in
cendisry bombs by Fascist in revenge
for Communist attacks. The explosion
caused great panic among the popu
lation, who fed into the open. The
entire building was destroyed.


PISA, Italy, May 8.-Three thousand
Nationalists from all parts of Tus-
cany gathered here yesterday to attend
the funeral of Signor Pacini, com
rade, who was shot by Communist,
While they were in this city large
number of Nationalists stormed
printing office where the publication
Anarchist Future and other subversive
sheets were issued. and set fire to the
premises.

The day of our deliverance from
the domination Of the janitor has
dawned. The doctrine that the jani-
tor can do no harm has dissolved
under police court test. A janitor
has been fined for disturbing the
peace. 1t has been decreed that
tenants have some rights which the
janitor is bound to respect.


This janitor. cherishing the conviction
general among janitors that the way
10 keep tenants humble Is to treat 'em
rough, made a great racket with a
waste basket on the back stairs and
beat on a tenants door and raised his
voice in janitor jargon and invited the
tenant to come out and have his head
knocked off. The tenant, being dis
Greet and desiring to retain his head,
remained inside until the janitor had
gone off somewhere and then came out
and had the king Of the apartment ar
rested and hailed into court like COM
mon culprit. And the judge. after hear
ing the evidence, fined him $100 and
laid down the law to the general effect
that janitors do not own the apart
ments and have no right to override
tenants rights.


Let all tenants take notice that the
courts of the land are open to them
in the struggle against the tyrannous
rule of the janitor. And let all janitors
beware lest the tenant worm, heart
ened by this courts action. turn to
the courts everywhere for relief from
the janitor's despotism.-St. Louis Post
Dispatch independently.

CLEVELAND, Feb. 17.-Two high
school teachers were beaten to death
with cudgels in desperate battle to
save their honor soon before nightfall
yesterday, in lonely spot in Parma
Township. suburb of Cleveland. They
were waylaid, assaulted and slain while
en- route to streetcar that would
take them to their homes.


The battered bodies Of the victims
Miss Louise Wolfe, thirty-seven years
old, and Miss Mabel Foote, twenty-four
were found by school children this
morning quarter mile from the
Parma rural school, where the women
were the only teachers. The bodies
had lain all night alongside little
used thoroughfare.


The only clew to the murderers are
footprints leading from the scene of
the double crime into q dense woods.


A posse of more than a hundred
farmers, armed with shotguns, revol-
vers or improvised weapons, are aid
ing Sheriff Stannard and his deputies
IN search of the entire township. A
deserted shanty on the border Of the
woods is believed to have been the
rendezvous Of the murderers. There
the posse found cigarette stubs, burned
matches and other evidence of recent
occupancy.


The search centers around two rough
~ dressed strangers who were seen
hurrying along Ridge Road less than a
mile from the scene of the attack at
dusk. Both were hatless and their
clothing was torn and mudstained.


Indications are that the women had
their battle in heavy downpour Of
rain soon before $3.50 o'clock yesterday
evening. The teachers were last seen
alive when they left the high school. q
few moments after O'clock.


The body of Miss Wolfe was living
near wire fence surrounding an or
chard. Her left arm covered her face
as though to ward off blow. Her
hands and face were badly swollen and
discolored. Eight feet away, face
down on the frozen earth, was the
body of Miss Foote She had been
battered almost beyond recognition
with heavy cudgels.


School books that had been carried
by the teachers were strewn along the
path of battle, and black handbag. in
the hands of Miss Foote, was crushed
and broken as though used as
weapon.


Not even the rings of the slain
women had been removed, and watch
carried by Miss Wolfe was still in
place. 1t had stopped at 5;15 o'clock.
The presence Of the rings and other
1ewelry disproved the first theory that
the motive was robbery.

LONDON, Dec. l. - A dispatch to
"The Times" from Tabriz, Persia,
dated Tuesday, says wild tribesmen
raided the American Lutheran Mission
at Syjbulak October and tore The
clothes off three Americans, the Misses
Schonhood, Fossum and Gudhard, and
brutally handled M. Bachir1ont, a
Frenchnaan attached to the mission.
Mrs. Bachimont was found two days
later in distraught condition, hiding
sin ruined house.


Five hundred gendarmes, who sur
rendered, were stood up In patches and
shot down with machine guns. After
These excuses the tribcsmen withdrew,
but no Persian troops had occupied
the town when the news reached here.
Two thousand gendarmes and cossacks,
however, were at Miandoab.


The raiders are part Of the forces
Of Simko, the Kurdish brigand chief,
who, making forced march from
Urumiah,- in the Province of Aver
baijan, appeared suddenly before Syj-
bulak October 6. The gendarmes re-
sisted the Kurds, but were defeated,
and on October Simko occupied the
town, which the tribesmen looted.

BERLIN, April 1.-THE en-
press is dead!"


The news from Doom that Au-
gusta Victoria has succumbed at
last to the heart disease which she
had gamely fought for months,
struck all Germany with the force
Of a stunning blow.


For, however, violently divided
may be the feelings about Wilhelm,
the woman who shared his joys
and sorrows for forty years and
stuck to him when all the world
showered hatred and abuse upon
his head, was beloved and reverred
by her former subjects.


BERLIN IN MOURNING.


Berlin was in deep mourning a few
hours after the news from Doorn had
reached here. Every now and again.
as Is the German custom, the church
bells tolled, solemnly, funereally. Sad
eyed newsboys are holding out black
bordered extra sheets bearing q briet
dispatch under the gigantic head
line:


Die Kaiserin Ist Tot"


Many of them bear the favorite pic
ture of the dead empress, surrounded
by her seven children aud several
grandchildren.


FUNERAL ON SATURDAY.


The Prussisn government ordered
the kaiserin's body to be brought into
Germany during the night, manifestly
fearing demonstrations. Burial will
take place Saturday morning. Every
precaution will be taken to prevent
demonstrations at railroad stations en-
route from Doom to Potsdam.

Let me tell you few of the big

some of which you may not realize.


Even in peace times the Navy's

our operations extended from our own

where they did yeoman service in con-

Nays activities literally belted the

one hundred and twenty submarine

Over 10000 officers and men of the

LONDON, July 30.-The deer of Ep-
ping Forest, to the northeast of Lon.
don, are disappearing, according to
the London letter of the Westminster
Gazette.


Forty years ago Epplng Forest con.
tanned three species of deer-the red
deer, the roe deer and the fallow
deer-and at one time they numbered
all told well over three hundred. Now
there are barely a hundred. practically
all fallow deer. All but three of the
red deer were captured some years
ago and transferred to Windsor Great
Park, and the remaining three had to
be destroyed, owing to their mischiev-
ious habits.


The roe deer were introduced TO Ep-
ping Forest about thirty.five years
ago, and at one time there were quite
thirty In the neighborhood of Monk
Wood; but six years ago the verderers
were able to discover barely half a
dozen.


For. some years after the City Cor
poration was made responsible for the
forest, m 1873, the fallow deer. then
numbering less than half a dozen, in
creased rapidly, and ten years ago
more than three hundred roamed the
forest north OF Chingford, bur now
that the motor-charabanc enables
trappers to reach this part of the for
est In large numbers. the fallow deer
are rapidly disappearing.

bond. They then walked quickly
from the bank only a moment before
the teller, Paul Purcell, returned TO
his cage. He Immediately missed the
bonds, but the men had left the
bank and disappeared.


Miss Esther Adams, who was in
the bank at the time, said she
watched the young men draw the
bonds from the cage. but feared to
cry out, not knowing whether they
were armed.

Associated Press) .--There was time
when Syzran was the most colorful
city along the Volga, but that time is
gone. To-day it is crowded with dust
begrimed peasants, who group them
selves into gray masses in their search
for food.

duplicated in Samara, Simbirsk, Sara
toll, Tzaritzin and every other city in
the famine stricken valley of the Volga,

high with the belongings of the ref
ugees, who were driven from their land

CHICAGO. December 2S.-A broad
view of the business situation in this
section shows both good and bad
indications, but the further the view
is extended into the future the more
cheerful conditions appear. the
trade in iron and steel is slack. but
the outlook for textiles and clothing
is hopeful Clothing makers are
looking for spring orders and retail
ers are clearing their stocks by bar
gain sales.


The banking and credit conditions
are better than they have been for
months. Large banks in the main
cities are out of debt to the reserve
bank and money rates are growing
easier. However. business needs
something besides easy credit. for old
debts cannot be discharged by max
ing commercial loans at banks. EASY
credit is for new business. but credit
conditions in this section are sound.


Retailers and distributors are pro-
ceeding with great care and are con-
cerned just now because the market
is frequently saturated with distress
goods sold by receivers far below
the market


There is little buying power in the
farming districts and it Is believed
there will be no great revival there
until another crop has progressed TAR
enough to insure returns. business
men and bankers agree that business
will be spotty for months to come.

HELSINGFORS, Finland. March 2S.-
Leaders of the soviet government who
for the last week or two have been
pushing vigorously their plans for the
immediate resumption of trade with the
western powers are now prepared to
make an extensive compromise with
capitalism.


They know that their country cannot
exist without help from the outside. and
hence they are willing to modify the
drastic military regulations within Rus
sia. allowing the cooperative societies
wider scope. giving the peasants the
right Of freer trade and removing the
main communistic obstacles to manu-
featuring and trade Of all kinds.


Willing to Take Chance.


It is apparent that Lenin realizes upon
whf delicate structure he is building
the new trade agreements. for in one of
his recent speeches he admitted that
recognition Of free trade closely re-
sembles the recognition of capitalistic
principles. However. he believes that
in the last three years all of Russia has
become deeply impregnated with COM
munism, and therefore he is willing to
take this chance.





under way for resum,ns trade with
Russia. The cooperative societies.
which are powerful throughout Finland.
are ready TO deal through the govern
ment with a soviet commission and will
probably furnish large quantities of
food. While the soviets keep Maxim
Litvinov in Reval, they intend using
other bases for commerce, especially the
Finnish ports which are usable for con-
signments of goods.


Offers Greater Freedom.


Having, as he thinks, completely paci-
fed Russia, Lenin now offers greater
political freedom. declaring that his
political adversaries have given him
greater latitude. All these statements
are interpreted by some conservative
observers as mere trickery, but it is
evident upon analysis that the soviet
dictators face crisis and have been
forced to modify their rules to prevent
disruption.

DOORN, Holland. April 16.-Former
Emperor William left the confines of
the grounds about Doom castle early
today and strolled in the village for
half hour. Ex-Crown Prince Frede-
rick William made several trips to
the Maarn railway station to inspect
the train that will bear the body of
former Empress Victoria to Potsdam
for burial.


Prince Henry OF Prussia, the for
mer emperors brother. and Prince
Fuerstenberg arrived here today.


Flags at Half-Mast.


POTSDAM, Germany. April 15.-
FIags of the old empire are flying at
half-mast along the strests of Pots
dam, and mourning bands are eVi-
dent on all sides. The shop windows
are displaying portraits of former
Empress Augusta Victoria, draped in
black. and flower pieces bearing her
insignia. Hundreds of individuals
and societies are honoring the mem
ory of the former queen. who will be
buried Tuesday next. with imperial
honors in the Antique Temple. ad-
joining the New Palace in Sanssouci
Park. where she lived virtually all
her married life.


Hundreds of persons formerly prom
Inent already are arriving in Potsdam,
which stands as an imperial oasis in
republican Germany. The former lord
chamberlain of the court. Count Au-
gust Won Eulenburg. has requisitioned
all hotels for those coming to attend
the funeral. The arrangements are
progressing under virtually the same
machinery as would have functioned
were the empire still intact.


Convert Into Chapel


Hundreds Of workmen are convert
ing the old imperial station at Wild
park into an embowered chapel in
which the family and immediate
friends of the late empress will re-
ceive the body and attend private
services before the procession starts
through the tree-lined lane leading
Immediately past the New Palace to
the temple. which will become the ex-
empress tomb.


Although Frederick the Great erected
the little temple for his own mauso-
leum. he is buried in garrison
church and the former empress will
be its first occupant.


The horse chestnut treeS in Sans
souci Park are in bud. the Towering
shrubs in bloom and the great court
lying between the New Palace and the
Temple is bright with beds of many
colored pansieS, among which the
body of the former empress will pass
on its way through the grounds,
where she was the recognized mis-
tress for 80 many years and where
she watched spring give its bright
touches to the somber forests and
gardens, dotted with white statues,
which need a background of foliage
to rob them of their coldness.

Cne Of the heaviest fogs that have
descended on New York in years was
blamed yesterday for streetcar col
ision at 1880 o'clock which injured
twelve persons and tied up traffic in
Graham Avenue, Brooklgn; held up
traffic in the ocean and bay and ham
pered the running Of elevated trains
and surface cars.


Slippery rails and fog caused the
Brooklyn mishap, when northbound
Graham Avenue car left the rails near
Stagg Street and plunged into south
bound car. A trailer behind the north
bound car left the rails with it and
more than 800 passengers were thrown
into confusion. Most Of the seriously
injured, however, were in the south
bound car, which was jammed from the
tracks and almost to the curb by the
force of the impact. Three OF those
hurt were taken to st. GATHERINGS
Hospital. The rest went home.


Police Lieutenant Convey. who was
passing, saw the crash and Immediately
summoned the reserves from the Stagg
Street station. These were followed by
reserves from Herbert Street and am
balances from st. GATHERINGS, Green
point and williamsburg hospitals. The
Rev. George Metzger, rector OF holy
Trinity Church, also responded.


Crowd Fights to Escape


The police and ambulance SURGEONS
found excited and hurt men and women
fighting to get out Of the wrecked ears.
Many broke windows and in that way
got to the street. Several, who were
only slightly hurt, refused medical at
tention and went home without giving
their names.


Fog and wet rails caused an east
bound Culver line elevated train to run
into "lay-up" train an hour later IN
the Van Siclen station, Coney Island.
The passengers in the Culver tram
were shaken up and several were cut
by flying glass. Two over were fron, srea'eo eoney by
Island Hospital.


The schedule of ferries to Manhattan
from Staten Island. Brooklyn and
Jersey was badly disarranged In the
early morning hours. Staten Island
ferries, which steer by compass. were
from ten to twelve minutes late be-
tween 7 and 8 o'clock. resulting In
congestion of trucks at St. George ana
the delay of many commuters: Erie
ferries from Jersey City to Twenty
third Street were suspended until
1880, though the Chambers Street line
was in operation slightly behind sched-
ule. West Shore ferries from Wee
hawken to Cortlandt Street were
twenty minutes behind schedule.

road got behind time when engineers

The Brooklyn ferries were even
harder hit than the Jersey boats. One
from Whitehall Street, Manhattan,
which left at a. n., did not reach
the slip at Thirty-nirth Street Brook,
lyn until an hour later. The norman
running time is twenty minutes.


Jersey Trains Delayed


The heavy fog blanket along the
railroad tracks in Jersey City delayed
through and suburban trains of the
Pennsylvania from half an hour to an
hour. it was reported, though it was
said at the Pennsylvania station that
as rule the trains arriving early In
the day had been on time.


The weather had held clear over the
lower bay and through Ambrose Chan
mel until early yesterday morning, when
the fog cloud let down like blanket
and persons at Quarantine could not
see ships hundred feet distant. Half
a dozen liners were tied up there for
several hours. Others were forced to
wait outside Sandy Hook.


More or less, fog has been hanging
about the city's waterways since Sat-
urdav afternoon. Meteorological sharps
account for it by saying that the un-
usually warm air coming in contact
with the cold sea water always makes
heavy and sticky mist.

records that before 1856, when topo-
graphical surveys were first under
taken, few geologic maps were pub
lished, but since that year the sur
veyors have added topography to

with a programme which will even
tually cover all the territory Of every
State. OF this ambitious programme
about 40 per cent. has been COM
pleted and published from engraved
plates. These have proved Of such
value to engineers and others inter
ested in industrial and transporta-
ton development that, as the Direc-
tor of the Survey, GEORGE OTIs SMITH,
writes, more speed is demanded"
Fortunately, the speed rate does not
depend wholly upon Congressional
aid, as several States are actively
cooperating with the Survey in this
work and in 1920 contributed total
CT nearly 100000"

veys of our neighbors New Jersey,
Connecticut and Rhode Island have
heen completed, and the plotting OF

MILAN, Italy, March 11.-Count Alva-

the noble families of Naples, commit

family palace in that city. In 1905 he
married the Countess Erminia Tore di
Santa Susanna, and they had two sons.
Two years ago the count and his wife
separated, and both went to Fiume,
where they got a divorce. This latter
was legally recognized in Italy, where
divorce laws DO not exist.


The count felt the separation keenly,
and revlsiting the old family home in
Naples, where his father and mother
still reside, he finally shot himself to
end his brooding misery. The bullet
lodged near the heart.


Although he lived for several hours
after the shooting, his only words were,
"Erminia, you have made me suffer-"
The divorced countess, hearing of the
tragedy, hurried to the hospital where
the dying man was. Holding out his
hand to her, he said: "Erminia, you
knew | still loved you. But | forgive
you and recommend you to my SON."


The tragic circumstances surround
ing the death and the final reconcile
alton have caused profound impress
sion IN Neapolitan society.

ployed away from home The dead
woman resided with Mrs. Coed.

means of a bent pipe.

military circles, high officers comment
ing that had the French General STAFF

British Foreign Minister, succeeded in

BOSTON. August s.-Sentiment in
business circles continues to improve
The feeling is growing that the worst
of the business depression is over
and that commodity prices in general
are on the up trend rather than in
danger of further decreases. Higher
prices for basic commodities haye
been shown in the last ten days. The
cotton goods market has shown de-
cidedly firmer tone and the demand
for fine goods. which has been strong
for a month, has spread to the lower
grades. Fall River mills still are sell
ing accumulated stocks around cost
of production. but decline to contract
for future deliveries except at ad-
vancing prices. Buyers are showing
disposition to follow the market up.


While the government wool auction
was unsatisfactory. less than half the
offerings being sold. wool here is in
fair demand, especially three-eighths
blood and the better grades. Woolen
cloth is selling well. especially light
weight offerings for spring delivery.


Department stores are buying goods
for future delivery rather more freely.
Paper patterns are selling better than
any other speciality. showing that
women are making their own clothes.
Piece dress goods are in great de-
mand.

were the toughest within their recol-

ALBANY. Feb. 1.-TWO snowballs
thrown at strikebreakers trying to ad-
just the trolley pole of a stalled car
here to-day started what threatened
for a time to be the worst riot that
this city has seen since the strike of
the employees OF the United Traction
Company began. Several thousand
persons followed the two snowballs.
probably thrown ny boys. with sticks
and stones and then rushed through
the detail Of police that was guarding
the stalled car. The battle ragged furi-
ously for several moments, but the
police finally drove the crowd back,
after cracking several heads with their
clubs, and escorted the car back to
the barns. No one was hurt seriously.


The crowd became so threatening,
even before II broke through the police
lines, that the city's entire force OF
traffic police-mounted, afoot and on
motorcycles---was mobllized in front
OF the State Capitol, where crowd OF
more than 1000 persons swarmed
about a street car and snow car

followed the car into State street, and
the snowbals were thrown when the
trolley pole lost contact with the wires.


Running from the swinging clubs OF
the police, hundreds of the crowd fed
down side streets TO block the car when
IL turned into Broadway. The motor
man swung the controller wide open
after leaving state street. however, and
by sheer speed. the strike breakers evaded
the crowd and reached the barns more
than a mile away.


The trouble to-day. which was the
largest so far as the number of partici-
pants are concerned that has developed
during the strike. started soon after
noon, when the strike breakers got in
sight of the state House with their
trolley car and the snow plough. They

grounds to use picks on a switch, and

Only three or four of them were using

jeers grew louder and louder. but the

break through the police lnss The

pathizers from tearing down trolley

II has been nearly forty years since
Anna Louise Cary's glorious voice
was heard by the American public. She
had been singing only little more
than ten years in opera and in con-
cert when she retired upon her mar.
riage. Since 1882 she has been liy-
ing a domestic life. almost all of that
time in Norwalk. Conn. Yesterday she
died. at the age of seventy nine, and
her death revives memories of old
times on the stage. Her name was
associated with those of the two PATHS.
Adelina and Carlotta: Nilsson, Gers
ter, Kellogg. Campanini and others
famous generation ago. Her voice
was remarkable contralto. of ex-
ceptional purity and range. She was
gifted with great beauty and her pres.
ence on the stage was magnetic. There
was genuine grief when she retired at
the age of forty, her voice undimin-
ished in its rare qualities. Perhaps
she was wise to stop then in the full
glory Of her talent and fame. Many
other singers have continued. some of
them beyond the point of discretion,
and the public has been kindly patient
for the sake Of memories. Anna Louise
Cary's voice still sounds in the mental
ears Of those who We're favored to
hear it. with the same purity and
depth and sweetness that were it's spe.
cial qualities when she sang her last
song on the stage

ELIZABETHTOWN. ILL.,. September
Slight hundred miners from Ell
dorado and nearby coal fields are
encamped within thirty miles of this
town, prepared to march on this city
and Rosiclare, leaders of the men told
who located their camp.


Reinforcements on the way from
the coal fields will bring the invading
army to more than 1000 men, 1t was
said.


Deputy sheriffs and private detec-
tives clashed with the outposts of the
miners. who held up two trucks and
three men at the Hog Thief's ford
on the Harrisburg road this after
noon. The miners retreated, leaving
four prisoners and three automobiles in
the officers hands.


Mines Closed for Months.


The difficulties in the southern
Illinois f1uorspar district date back
almost year to strike called in
and Hillside companies by the In
ternational Union of Mine. Mill and
Smelter Workers.


Local union officials claimed 914
members, but mine owners asserted
they never employed more than 900
AhcIi Iii tnTee mines anu tldt HOl
more than 200 of these men Joined
the unions. Many of the union mem
bers. county officials said, were small
hill farmers, fishermen and mer-
chants, who had Joined the union to
get the free rations issued weekly
by the strike committee


Mine owners have not been attemnt-
ing to operate for several months,
saying the available supply of mined
spar was sufficient for all demands up
to next May.


Eight Shot Last Week.


Friction between strikers and the
mine guards resulted in shooting at
Rosiclare ten days ago. when eight
persons were wounded. For week the
situation was quiet, but a few days
ago women and children left or were
driven from Rosiview. another town
in the district. Union officials said
armed mine guards threatened the
town, compelling the women to flee;
county officials declared the flight
was staged by union organizers to
gain sympathy.

growing more tense, without actual
outbreak thus far. All available citi-
zens of Rosiclare and EliZabethtown

Burglars who had defed the police
to catch them, naming the address they
intended to visit, were captured yes
terday by detectives who took the dare.


Last January gang Of expert safe
openers entered the loft building at
338 Canal Street, ripped open safes
there and departed after collecting
$4,000 in jewelry and unset precious
stones. No policeman interfered with
them. Detectives who were summoned
after the harm had been done made no
progress toward arresting the cracks
men, who, flushed with pride over their
easily accomplished feat, gave way to
boasting.


These boasts sounded through the
underworld and eventually came to the
ears of the police. Stool pigeons in
formed Captain John j. Stapleton, head
Of the loft and safe squad, that the
mob" that had gone through the
Canal Street building were laughing at
him and his efforts to find them. That
made Captain Stapleton angry.


Later, the doughty captains wrath
became apoplectic when certain stink
ing persons whispered to his men that
the same vainglorious gang of "yeggs"
were loudly announcing their intention
of visiting the same loft building all
over again, collecting whatever tney had
missed on their first visit and enjoying
another hearty laugh at the expense of
the sluggish police.


Patience Is Rewarded


Whereupon the safe and loft squad,
from captain to youngest member,
swore mighty oath to catch these
braggarts if it was the last act of their
official lives. After the challenge was
carried to them, the detectives did not
relax their vigilance over the building
for an instant. Weeks passed and
story of the city's crime the loft
burglary in Canal Street was forgotten
by most persons. But Stapleton and
his men remembered it with the tenac-
ity and vindictiveness Of affronted cle-
plants.


Yesterday their long watch had its
reward They knew the "safe mob"
was about to fulfill it's threat, for de-
tective watching the building from the
outside several days ago saw q furtive
figure slip up to the door and take a
wax impression of the keyhole.


At 3 o'clock yesterday afternoon





key made from that impression. saun-
tered up to the building, which had
been closed since noon, and entered
They ascended to the fourth floor
Behind them crept several members of
the safe and loft squad with the caution
of cats.


Valuable Stock Saved


The trio paused before the office Of
S. Steinberg, manufacturing jeweler, in
whose safe there reposed some 100000
worth of gems and metals. The Office
door has a patent lock. The three cut
this away and entered. The safe in the
corner had yielded $1,000 at the time
of the January robbery. 1t held much
greater treasure now, but the trio
made no attempt to open it, They
placed black bag one of them carried
before it, and then started back down
stairs. Evidently they were merely
getting ready for long nights work.


They walked smack into the arms of
waiting detectives. who fell upon them
with all the violence inspired by
long-pent-up emotions. 1t was good
fight while it lasted, but the trio were
outnumbered and overpowered.


In the black bag the triumphant
sleuths discovered three sticks of dyna-
mite, set of drills of the finest steel,
brace, one of the best constructed
sectional jisnmies the police have ever
seen, and three pairs of gloves.


At headquarters the three were
charged with burglary, attempted burg
larry and possessing dynamite illegally
They were booked as Joseph Marcus,
alias Joseph Simon; Harry Gold, alias
Aaron Gold, 229 East Eighteenth
Street, and Harry Salkin, 31l South
Fifth Street, Brooklyn.


Captain Stapleton was smiling last
night for the first time in three months.

widely spread report that he trains
on beer and cigarettes. He observes
virtually the same training rules that

NoRwALK. Conn.,. Dec. 7.-Charles
kenney, keeper Of Norwalk light, went
out into Long Island Sound in a row.
boat early this morning with his as
sistants, George H. Barker and George
Clark, and rescued four men of the
crew Of the steam canaler J. C. Austin
of Brooklyn. The quartet had been
drifting about off shore In high seas
since their ship went down in a ter
rifle gale early last night. All suffered
severely from exposure. while one,
George Westergaarten of Perth Am
boy, a fireman. was SO badly burned
that he is not expected to live.


The others rescued were Capt. Joseph
Byers. commander of the Austin;
Charles Walker, engineer, and Walter
Warren, cook, all of Brooklyn. With
Westergaarten they tried to keep the
Austin from sinking by working the
pumps, and at the same time they
tried to launch their lifeboat a difficult
task because of the high seas sweep
ing and plunging over the rail Of the
ship. During this work pipe in the
boiler burst and there was great dan
ger that the boiler would explode be-
fore the boat could be launched.


Westergaarten volunteered to repair
the break. Throwing wet ashes on the
fires, he crawled into the hot boiler to
find the leak. But the fires had not
gone out and he was burned so badly
within a few minutes that he became un-
conscious and was not able to cry fo-
help. But after some time. while Wes-
tergaarten was slowly roasting to death,
Capt. Byers became alarmed.


Drag Out Roasting Fireman.


He opened the boiler. and after great
trouble and danger he and the two
other men managed to get inside and
drag the body of the fireman into the
engine room. Westergaarten was unable
to help himself or make even an effort
to save his life.


The ship was beginning to settle by
this tine. Capt. Byers carried Wester-
gaarten to the deck. while Walker and





scme time. managed to get the lifeboat
over the side. Fortunately the boat was
not swamped as she hit the waves. Capt.
Byers clambered down the side into the
lifeboat with the body of Westergaarten
in his arms, followed quickly by the cook
and the engineer. Two or three minutes
after they had cast off the Austin went
down by the bow.


Capt. Byers and the two other men Of
his crew had not had time 20 get food
before they jumped into the lifeboat. and
they wore only their shirts and trous-
ers. as the work with the pumps and in
the engine and boiler rooms had been
hot and fatiguing and they had dis
carded their outer clothing. The wind
was blowing a gale, and although they
rowed hard they were not able to make
the shore. Throughout the night they
drifted. managing with great effort to
keep within sight Of the beams OF the
lighthouse.


Lifeboat Drifting to shore.


When morning came the lifebost with
the burned man and the three others I'm
1t was drifting slowly In to shore. Their
distress signals were seen by Keeper
Kenney of the light and he went out
with his aids. the high seas having gone
down by that time Suf1cfently to enable
them to launch a small boat without
much difficulty Kenney found Capt.
Byers and his men half frozen. with the
unconscious Westergaarten covered with
their shirts, while the others tried 10
handle their boat with no warmer cloth
ing than their underwear.


The strength OF the shlpwrecked men
as so far gone that they never would
have been able to row their lifeboat to
shore, and their only chance, if the light
house keeper had not rescued them.
would have been passing vessel. They
had drifted so far inshore that there
would have been little likelihood that
they could have been rescued. But
Keeper Kenney with Barker and Clark.
transferred them to the lighthouse boat.
and then. after much work, managed to
lift them up The iron sides OF the light
house and 20 safety.


Inside the lighthouse Kenney gave
Capt. Byers and his men warm clothing
and food and did what he could for Wes-
tergaarten. Distress signals were flown
from the lighthouse. but II was some
hours before the seas and the gale had
gone down sufficiently for boat to an
swer them. Finally Capt. Stanley Tall
n adge put his oyster steamer alongside
the lighthouse and took Capt. Byers and
his men off. Capt. Tallmadge carried
them to Norwalk, where they we're sent
TO a hospital.

Americans.

effect on the exchange rate and the
sales during the fair. which will con-
tinue seven days. The fair is the
largest in the eight hundred years it

temporary buildings. The streets have

CHICAGO, Jan. 17.-Mrs. Cleopatra
McGory HUFFMAN, twenty years old,
confessed tonight that she was the
woman lure for band of hold-up men,
led by her young husband, and that she
had participated in more than fifty
hold-ups in the last two months. Her
husband and another alleged member
of the gang are under arrest.


The woman was arrested to-day in
South Peoria street residence, where
she had taken. a position as house
keeper when the police chase became
warm.


In bored. cynical tone and with the
sophistication of her celebrated name
sake She told how she managed her
victims in the hotel and restaurant
district and led them to where her hus-
band and his fellow bandits waited for
the spoils.


Just Simple Country Girl


"To begin with" she said languidly,
evidently enjoying herself, 81 was a
simple country girf." Then with a
sigh of retrospection, she murmured: {:
at was SO easy getting the money from
the chumps that l often wondered why
l spent twenty years on the farm"
According to her story, she had
passed the greater part of her life on
farm near Wichita Falls, Tex. She
married farmer, and when he died
she went out into the world, leaving
her two children with relatives At Har-
low, Okla. She joined a carnival com
pany, and was one of the dancing girls
in days of '49' show Then she
came to Chicago. became waitress and
married Kurt Hurtzman. She said he
lost his health and they decided to be-
come bandits.


"They are all the same-these men,"
she said, registering the conventional
vampire. Each of them laid the trap
for himself. Some promised me furs.
diamonds and motors" and she yawned
slightly.


Kiss for Each Victim


II laughed. in my sleeve and led
them to the darkened hallway where
Kurt and his gang waited. ! always
kissed them once we left them alone,
tied up in room in strange place.
she continued.


She explained that she would walk
along the street. watch out for u pros
porous looking man and then tell hins
she was lost. She would tell him she
wanted to go to a certain address, and
when he would explain that it was
only short distance away, 81 brought
forth a smile and generally he would
volunteer to accompany me-


Each was the superior being
ready to take advantage of a woman,
and each was properly fooled" She
concluded, and registered the satiated
vampire look which indicates deep sat
isfaction after victim has met his
doom.

Twenty thousand persons conrre-
gated in front of the Public Library.
IN Bryant Park and adjacent streets
late last night to witness an auction
OF jobless men and women which had
been promised by Urbain Ledoux. auc-

Fifth Avenue, between Forteth and

By III o'clock the gathering was so

cult to handle that all available police

occasion. Clubs we're used here and

Where's Ledoux ?" was one slogan

We want Zero-Mis-ter Zero" was
another.


Groups that had congregated on the

persed and an announcement made bv
Captain Howard that Ledoux would not
appear. 1t became known that "Mr.
Zero" after his exciting experience at

James Fagan, of the bomb squad, that he
would abandon the plan for an auction
az the library at night. The crowd be,
beved that Ledoux had been placed
under arrest and shouts were heard
condemning the police for this action.


The curious began congregating soon
after o'clock. At that hour Bryant
Park was filed with men who appeared
to be of the working class. Early COM
ers occupied benches, but every yard
of grass was tramped into the dust be-
fore another hour had elapsed. Hun
dreds arrived from all directions on
II trains. subways, surface cars and
in automo obiles. BEFORE dark the park
and its approaches were in possession
of q milling crowd.


More. than two hundred passengers
ahghted fron, the Sixth Avenue al"
train at Forty-second Street and

station, refusing to move on and block

When Inspector Boettler ordered

Howard, with 100 men, advanced
through the several gates and ordered
"all out" This was the signal for a
demonstration on the part of the mob
that had every appearance of prear
rangement.


Police Clear Bryant Park


The hundred patrolmen closed in
from three sides and gradually worked
the throng out of Bryant Park, han
ding reluctant ones with great good
nature, but taking no back talk from
truculent individuals encountered here

In spite Of police efforts to keep the
crowd in motion congestion continued
to increase until II o'clock, when $50
patrolmen and sixty detectives were
engaged in an attempt to disperse the
multitude. North bound pedestrians in

south bound the west. More than 200
patrolmen were necessary to maintain
this order in force between Fortieth

necesstating reinforcements of police
at certain points.


After the police had dispersed the

thence to Central Park where speeches
were made near the Maine monument
denouncing "police brutality" and de-
manding fair treatment for men who
had served in the war. This meeting
also was dispersed by the police, most
of the men taking refuge in Central
Park.

men who had been sleeping in Bryant

masked men early to-day boarded

weston The highwaymen escaped

English ex-service men prefer war to

Legion in the war against the Moroccan
tribes. The recruiting campaign had

checked suddenly because there were far
more applicants for enlistment than

said Spain wanted only war veterans.

and decorations stormed the Consulate
in such numbers that the queue in
Bloomsbury looked like an army of suf-
ficient size to subdue all Morocco.


In the queue waiting for a chance to
apply for enlistment were many men
who had been driven there by hunger
and other discouraging conditions. but
also in the vast number there were
many who were simply adventurers.
These latter were mostly young men
who were trying to escape from the
drab monotony OF civilian life. They
were willing to fight the Moors and the
Riffs or anybody else anywhere. 50 long
as thrill was promised them.


But the acceptances were compare
tively few because the Spanish trans
port, Almiranto Lobo, at Southampton
was unable to accommodate anything &

HARRINGTON, Mo-, May 19.-Charged

years old, the Baby Bride of the
Ozarks," stood at the bar of justice
here to-day.


Although Letta is without friends to
comfort her, public opinion is solidly
behind her. Letta was born and reared
in the ozarks and was deserted BIZ her
parents when an infant. She can
neither read nor write. She has lived
around from one place to another"
cooking, sweeping. washing and taking
care of some one else's children for her
board and place to sleep.


Into her life came John Parsons. the
wood chopper of Iron Mountain. she
saw chance to get out of always work
ing for some one else. She married
Parsons, who was much older and had
two children, Lilly and John .jr., by a
former marriage.


Five days after the marriage she
shot and killed Lilly with a shotgun.
She admits the shooting, but she de-
clares. she did not know the gun was
loaded. John jr. testified at the iraue st
that Letta and Lilly quarreled when
Letta wanted to comb Lilly's hair. LiIIy
tried to run away, according to the boy.
and Letta got the gun and shot her.

stop that foolingl You will upset

Refugees reaching London from
Russia tell vivid stories of the decay
of Petrograd.


Hundredsaof thousands have left
the once prosperous Russian capital.
Now the remaining population num-
bers only 100000, two-thirds OF
whom are women.


Madame Struve, wife of Baron
Struve, Wrangers foreign minister,
was one of the recent Russian
refugees who passed through Lon
don. She had escaped from the
north of Russia after enduring many
hardships.


She described how the wooden
buildings of Petrograd are all being
torn down for fuel; how the wooden
pavements are fast disappearing,
because the freezing inhabitants
steal the wooden blocks for their
stoves.


Many homes are in darkness be-
cause there are no candles, and the
municipal lighting system runs only
a couple of hours a day.


Mortality has reached a startling
rate. So-called healthy" people
have faces of wax-like color and
suffer from starvation dropsy, which
changes the expression of faces so
that one can scarcely recognize old
acquaintances. Those who are ,classed
as sick" have such maladies as
spotted fever, smallpox, influenza,
abdominal and intermittent typhus
and pneumonia.


People die on operating tables
from severe cold OF the unheated
hospitals and from neglect and from
shortage of hospital essentials un-
procurable in Russia, the refugees
reaching London declare. Houses
are rapidly becoming uninhabitable.
Once the plumbing breaks it is
usually impossible to have 1t re-
paired. The family lives in the house
till it becomes too filthy and then
moves out barring the doors

gayeVthe river its melodious name,

onists during the French and Indian

From the same old fighting
ground Daniel Morgan conducted
his operations against the British
thu civil war, the valley was fought
over repeatedly.


Meets Pike ut winchester.

Potomac River. breaking through

Shenandoah, and where memories OF
John Browns Inflated expedition
Iinger, the motorist strikes the VAL
ley Pike at Winchester, famous as

heroic ride, as the site of Fort Lou
don, built by Gen. Washington after
Braddock's defeat. as the burial
place of Gen. Morgan, the headquar-
tiers of Stonewall Jackson, and Of
such strategic Importance during
the civil war that the town is re-
puted to have changed hands no
less than seventy-two times.


Kearnstown, Middletown, Stras-
burg. Woodstock. Edinburg. Mount
Jackson and New Market all have
historical associations connected
with the colonial. Revolutionary or
civil wars and all of them lie along
the broad Valley Pike which was
chartered In 1887 and has since been
Incorporated with the National
highway.

The final legislative step for the
outlawing of beer and malt liquors
for medical purposes was taken to-
day by the Senate.


By vote of 56 to 90 the Senate
adopted the conference report on the
so-called anti-beer bill and the meas
ure now goes to the President, the
House having acted some time ago.


Twelve republicans and ten demo-
Gratis voted against the conference
report.


How They Voted.


The republican opponents were Sem

SON tCalif.), La Toilette, Lodge, Nc
Lean. Penrose, Phipps, Shortridge.
Wadsworth and Weller. The demo-
Gratis were Senators Broussard, Gerry.
King, Pomerene, Ransdell, Shields,
Stanley, Underwood, Walsh (Mass)
and Watson (Gs.).


Two others. Senators Reed. demo-
crat, Missouri, and Moses. republican.
New Hampshire. were paired against

Thirty-three republicans and TWEEN

sofa: Lenroot. republican. Wisconsin.
Mccormick, republican. Illinois; Suth-
erland, republican, West Virginia, and

Effect Of Action.
The bill will set aside the ruling by
Former Attorney General Palmer.
who, two days. before he retired. ad-
yised the prohibition enforcement of
ficials that there was nothing in the
volstead act to prohibit the prescrip-
ton of beer and light wines for
medicinal purposes.


The anti-beer legislation has been
before Congress since last June. The
House accepted the compromise reach
| ed by the conferees in August, but
there followed a bitter controversy in
the Senate, waged by a small but de-
termined group, who contended that
the bill struck a fatal blow at per-
sonal rights because it permitted
search and seizure without warrants.
The first draft of the measure au-
| thorized the search OF private homes
without warrants. but this feature
was eliminated in conference.
Prescriptions Are Limited.
The bill limits physicians to 100
prescriptions for liquor each three
months and specifies that not more
than a quart Of spirituous or vinous
liquor containing in the aggregate
lot more than one-half pint of alcohol
may be prescribed for one person in
ten days.


Importation Of liquors is barred by
the bill until the supply on hand in
the United States shall no longer be
sufficient to meet the current need for
non-beverage uses.

Berlin, July 10.


The stock exchange activity reported
last week continues. This is partly due
to the increase in German industry fol-
lowing the recent Quotations of the mark
and gradual depreciation. The talk of a
general industrial depression is abating
and regular orders are again coming in.
Trade which tottered at one time is now
resuming, and finished wares. where the
demand diminished, are finding ready
market again The world market crisis
produced slow paralysis of German
industry rather than collapse, causing
firms to so on the rocks. Few German
firms, in fact, have succumbed to the de-
preston.


The home market, through want Of
buying and carrying capacity, remains
restricted, but outside orders are again
coming in. The higher value of the
mark and higher world market prices
again permit the Germans to undersell
foreign manufacturers in wool, cotton
and leather goods. Modification of Ger
man industries continues. The Rhine
Metallic Works and Machine Company
and also the Wolf Works and the Treven
Rolling Mills are forming combine. and
the steel combines and coal and iron in
terests arc reported to be investing heav-
lily in ship building shares again.


The Industrial outlook has improved
this last month. Unemployment has de-
creased slightly owing to the resumption
Of building. The Rhenish coal and iron
industries have received heavy home and
foreign orders, owing to the Upper Sile-
sian upheaval.

Princeton football team rolled up four
touchdowns and two field goals
against the University Of Virginia
in the Palmer Stadium this after
noon, defeating the Southerners by
the score of "a to 0. All four OF
the Tiger touchdowns came in the
first two periods, when the regular
varsity was intact, but the Virginians
held well In the last two periods,
end the Orange and Black scoring
was confined to two pretty field goals
from the toe of Ken Smith.


The visiting team was unable to
stop the Princeton attack in any
department OF the game. the pass
ing OF the Tigers being most effective
in producing scores. Capt. Keck won
the toss from Rlnehart, the Virginia
leader, and elected to receive the
kick-off. The first score came ~
result of bautiful forty-yard run
by Jack Cleaves which put the bail
on the courtyard line. He was thrown
for a two-yard loss on the next play,
but Clarity plunged through center
for the score, and Keck kicked the
goal The next Princeton touchdown
came when Capt. Rinehart. Of the Virs
ginians. fumbled and Snively pecoy-
cred the ball for the Tigers in the
middle Of the field. Cleaves ripped
on another long run, this time for
twenty-five yards. and on the next
play Garrity scored in the corner
OF the field after receiving Van
Gerbig's long pass.


Passes Increase Total.


The Orange and Black touchdowns
In the second quarter both came from
forward passes. the first being made
by Hank Clarity, who received from
Snively. and the second by Peck
Euwer on a very short pass over the
center of the line by Van Gerbig.
Euwer was waiting for the twisting
oval on the good side of the goal
line.


The Virginians had only one
real chance to score, and that was
in the first part of the last quarter,
Two fifteen-yard penalties took
the pigskin back we'll within
Princeton territory for the first
time during the game. The South
erners then opened their only sue
cessful attack of the afternoon, by
series of forward passes from
open formation. and completed fve
out of their six attempts. The last
heave was from Foster to Opple-
man and the latter was brought
down within one foot of the Tiger
goal line. On the next play Vir-
gtnia was offside and was sent
back five yards. Foster dropped
back on the next lineup and tried
another. of the passes which had
heretofore been so successful, but
the heave was wild and the ball
was grounded behind the Princeton
goal posts.


The hearts of the Princeton root
ers came back to normal beating,
for Virginia never opened up her
attack to any dangerous degree
again during the game. Both
teams had put in a great number
OF Substitutes and there was very
little interesting playing after that
except the brilliant kicking of
Smith. Smith was the second sub
stitute used for Jack Cleaves and
undoubtedly supported the judg-
ment of the coaches. His first boot
was from the 45-yard line and the
second from S5-yards. The line
helped him in both attempts by
holding well.


LOurie Fails to Play.


Coach Bill Roper evidently did
not want to run the chance of
Lourie's hurting his leg again and
thus be out of the Harvard and
Princeton games for the Tiger
backfleld ace warmed the substi-
tutes throughout the entire game.
Lourie had been drilling all week
with the varsity and the expecta-
ton of the undergraduates was
that their idol would be in the play
today, but the dope was upset.
Jack Cleaves was easily the most
prominent star of the Tiger ma
chine this afternoon. He made
long. Jagged runs through broken
fields for twenty-five and forty
yards respectively in the first quar-
ter, each of which placed the pig
skin in a good position for the
score which followed. Garrity
again was in the form that has won
for him the high reputation he has
as a plunging back. Besides, his
consistent gains through the line
he called the signals from quar-
terback and showed admirable
leadership.


Rutan Defensive Star.


The defensive work Of Frank Rutan,
who was substituted for "Whoop'
Snively at left end, was nothing short
OF miraculous. Time after time he
stopped the Virginia backs behind
their own line, and his showing Is all
the more creditable because he has
always been-a tackle before this week
Strangely enough. a substitute back
was the Outstanding light on the
Southern combination. Foster took
Carrington's place at quarterback in
the first period and was the power Of
the visitors passing attack. as well

tercepted several Princeton passes,
running them back for good gains.
Capt Rinehart did the punting for

the Tiger readily broke through the
Southern forwards. The superiority

and Virginia five. Virginia threatened
only once. when 80 yards of penalties
brought them within range. The
Orange and Black was penalized for

ATLANTIC CITY, May 30,--With n
four-days' rest awaiting him Jack
Dempsey took his last workout to-day
until Saturday, stepping six furious
rounds with three sparring partners.


The workout was witnessed by the
largest crowd that his jammed the
champions open air arena since he
started training two weeks ago. There
were several hundred women spectators
and they gave Dempsey round of
applause after he finished.


Larry Williams, the 180-pounder, who
was all but knocked out yesterday, re-
ceived another battering this after
noon. Dempsey punished him unmer-
left hooks, occasionally Strengthening
HIM up with solid smashes to the head.


Partner Fights Back


Williams is proving the best sparring
partner for the champion, as he fights
back all the time, while the others
content themselves by backing away
from Dempsey's rushes. Dempsey
opened up the cut over Williams's right
eye with the last punch of their ses-
sion.


After Williams left the ring Jack
Renault and Leo Houck faced the
champion 1Of TWO ToUuuS edCU, uu
Dempsey was unable to do much with
them because of their inclination to
retreat.


Dempsey cracked Renault twice on
the chin with left hooks and dug left
into his body without a return, but
Jack sent Houck to his launches with
straight left in the first round he
boxed.


Champions Wound Healing


Dempsey wore full length tights in
stead Of fighting trunks, as a chill
wind swept off the ocean and he did
not want to risk the danger Of catch
ing cold. He also wore strip Of white
court plaster over his right eye to pro
tect it. The wound, opened when
Dempsey's head collided with Renault
on Friday, is healing nicely.


Despite another threatening down
pour and rain-soaked roads, Dempsey
insisted on covering six miles on the
road this morning. While trotting
along with his three dogs, a passing
motorist struck CDR Hemingway" one
of the champions Belgian police dogs
running over the animal and stun
ming it.


When the motorist brought his cal
to stop and learned the identity OF
the champion he quickly blurted out
an apology. Dempsey rushed over to
the injured dog, picking him up in his
aims. The dog was not seriously hurt
and managed to limp back to the camp
with the champion.

Of Lord Mount Stephen, or, as Can

Ames brothers, Oliver and Oakes
and Charles Francis Adams of the
Union Pacific, and Cyrus Holiday
the father of the Atchison, died years

beginning of this century.


They were all big men, big in head
and heart, men who could see vast
opportunities, conceive great projects
and carry them through despite al
the obstacles which nature or their
financial rivals placed in their way
Many of them went into the West
when II was raw and new. George
Stephen went from Scotland to Can
ada when it scarcely was more than
making a start. Donald Smith, az
the New World then knew Lord
Strathcona, went into the almost
unknown north and served years OF

Company before he finally became
one Of its resident governors. Hun
tington, Hopkins, Stanford and
Crocker went to the Pacific coast in
the early gold days, Holiday was on
the Kansas prairies when the Terri
tory was the bone of contention be
tween the Jayhawkers and the pro
slavery men, and Hill had settled in

Minneapolis were villages.

servation and from contact with the
people the country over which they
were to build their roads. They not
only spanned the nation with iron

of it's transportation, from the bark

Our first transcontinental railway
the Union Pacific, was brought be
fore the public as far back as 1S46
when Asa Whitney began making
addresses upon the subject before
State legislatures and memorializina
Congress. Work was begun in 1858

ward from California and the Unior
Pacific Company building westward
from Omaha. Huntington was the
fiscal agent of the Central Pacific

portion, for the Central was well vi

miles of the Union Pacific from

met at Promontory Point, Utah, a
point 600 miles east of Sacramento
and 1854 miles west Of Omaha. Th,
last tie. a piece of laurel wood from
California, was put in position, sill
yer spike presented by Nevada and
one of iron, silver and gold furnished
by Arizona were driven and then came
"the last spike" one Of gold given by
California. Five days later through
trains began running over the road
the first transcontinental service.


The next transcontinental line:
were the Southern Pacific, finished In
1881, from San Francisco to New
Orleans; two years later, the North
ern Pacific from st. Paul to Portland
Oregon; then the Atchison, Topeka
and Santa Fe from Kansas City tc
San Diego, followed by the Great
Northern from st. Paul to Seattle and

STATE COLLEGE, Pa. Jan. Nineteen
twenty-one promises to be a mighty busy
athletic year all over the country. and
this Is particularly the case at Penn
State, where Hugo 'Bezdek has been
spending his Christmas holidays in deep
meditation as to the ways and means
by which he can give the Blue and
White institution another upward push
on the ladder of success. The director
Of athletics Is out to make the new year
even more successful than the one just
checked off by Father Time.


But Bendek will have some job on his
hands to better the record made by
Penn State teams during 1920. With
undefeated football and soccer teams
and with only one contest lost in basket
ball. wrestling and boxing respectively,

one games and was ranked with Lafay-
cite as the best team in the East. Nor

Martins men won four dual meets,

and registered three firsts-including the
distance medley and four mile relay
championships-two seconds and third
at the Penn relays. During the indoor
season the medley relay team broke the
indoor record at the Johns Hopkins
games and also won the medley race
at Buffalo. The cross country team de-
feated Penn In the only dual meet Of
the season, while "Blondy" Romig, the
Penn State captain. romped home a WIN
ner at the intercollegiate cross country
championships over the Yale course.

winning the Berwick marathon after
outdistancing several runners who COM
peted in the Olympic games. Harold
Barron and Larry Shields, two of Mar
tins aces, represented Penn State at the
Olympic contests. and both men we're
the first Americans to finish in their re-
spective events, Barron forcing Earl
Thomson. the famous Canadian hurdler,
10 break the worlds record in order to
win.

part in only two contests. and they
earned an even break. The tennis team

MESSINA, Italy, June 20 (By The
Associated Pressl.-The volcano Strom-
boli, on Stromboli Island, off the north
coast of Sicily, burst into wild activity
last night and terror fills the island
The molten rocks and sulphurous gases
pouring from the crater, it is feared,
may spell impending doom to the
panic-stricken inhabitants.


The people of the island, frenzied
by the uncanny behavior of the volcano
during the last three days, are congre-
eating on the shores preparing for an
attempt at fight, but waiting in the
hope that the volcano Will subside.


The eruption is accompanied by
earthquakes, felt for thirty miles,
shaking the adjacent islands. Flames
and black clouds from the volcano
are plainly seen from Messina. The

VIENNA, Oct. % tBy The Asso-
ciated Press ).-Charles, former
King of Hungary, entered Budapest
this afternoon, according to report
telephoned here from Prague. This
is not confirmed from other sources.
All wires between Vienna and Hun
gary have been cut.


Earlier dispatches reported that
Charles and his forces had reached
Budaors, seventeen miles from the
Hungarian capital, where sharp
fighting was in progress this after
noon. Admiral Horthy, regent Of
Hungary, was reported to be person.
ally leading the troops against
Charles.


Budapest Hears Cunfire


The forces of Charles were said to
aggregate several battalions. They
arrived at Budaors early tbs morn
ing. The sound of the guns was au-
dible in, Budapest.


At Budaors Charles's advance had
been checked, one of the dispatches
saying that the train that preceded
Charles had reached that place, but
was forced to back out hurriediy upon
show of resistance by the govern
ment troops.


fha - -
is known beyond doubt that there
has been brisk, and possibly sangui-
nary, fighting close to Budapest.


A telephone message from Prague
said that Charles had succeeded in
reaching Budapest, while the Vienna
"Freie Presse" announces that the Ital-
ian Legation has received news from
Budapest that some of the troops in
that capital have declared in favor OF
Charles.


Reinforcements for Ex-King


Oedenburg, Steinamanger and Stahl-
weissenburg troops, it is declared, are
Fastening to reinforce the ex-king, and
the fact that bloodshed has begun ts
believed by those who know the Hun
garian character to foreshadow a final
grapple between the reactionary and
the republican forces that probably
will extend beyond the borders.


Though possibly checked, the mon
archists are evidently concentrating
for further attacks, for latest, though
meagre, advices say that the battle
between the monsrchists and govern
ment troops continues, and also that
the behavior of the government forces
is irreproachable.


Government circles hope to be able
to hold out until the arrival of rein
forcements from the provinces, which
are expected tomorrow afternoon.


Insurgent bands from Burgenland
are reported to be marching to the sup
port Of Charles. An Oedenburg dis
patch to the "Tageblatt" gives the re-
port of the resignation of the Bethlen

noMaS, III discussing the ACCIDENT,

Fiume has recalled public attention to
Italy. Since the war, Italy has been
largely forgotten. She has not asked for
outside help. She has sent out no appeals.


She has cared for her own people. She
has fed and clothed them and provided
them work. She has had serious internal
troubles, but has known her own people.
and has solved them.


In a vast part of her north and north
eastern country beyond the Piave, the
destruction was comparable to that of
Flanders and Northern France. Italy has
had this enormous problem of reparation.


According to recent reports those cities
have been restored in every instance to at
least 20 per cent and in many as much
as 60 per cent This same systematic re-
storation has extended to the rural dis
tricts


Nor did any country suffer more in pro-
portion, financially and in man power.
Never rich, her gold reserves were largely
in German hands and were withdrawn after

prison authorities and learned that

teen years from Bergen county for a
similar crime, were missing.

animated at the outset. but in the later
part of the forenoon died down con-
siderably. The South sold, as did Wall

hardly sufficient to take care of all
offerings in the market. There was
no change in sentiment. which con-
tinued mixed. New business was re-
stricted by a little professional short
selling. The trade took few lots on
the call, but later left the market.


Demand for cotton goods was re-
ported as very quiet, and the tone of

heaviest pressure was not met until

dropped more than 20 points. Pressure

finish Final bids were 10 to Is points

Any man who caught himself
cutting his tire tread with a file
would voluntarily apply for admis-
sion TO the nearest retreat for the
feeble-minded. Yet the same man
will lock his brakes and slide ten
feet and think nothing about it.
Too many motorists confuse
their tires with skates. Instead of
looking ahead for obstacles and
checking the car slowly by closing
the throttle with the clutch en-
gagged, they wait until they are
right in the middle of an emer-
gency and then jam on the brakes.
They never stop to consider these
little slides with the brakes locked
until they notice spots where the
tire tread is worn through to the
fabric.


Even where the tread is not
scraped through to the fsbric, tire
men point out that there are flat
places left in the tread. Them. as
the car proceeds, these flat pieces
pound away on the road like a
flat-wheeled trolley, killing the
mileage in the tire.


Letting in the clutch too quickly,
spinning the back wheels in mud
holes, taking corners at high speed
and locking the brakes means a
short life for tires.

To the north rose a gentle hill: to the west

ness and baroness to the fields about the

PARIS. June lO.-The ugly atti-
tude of the peasants, mutinies
among the soldiers. and the grow
ing scarcity of food have instilled
a fear among bolshevist officials
that the dissolution of the soviet
regime is imminent, according to
French foreign Office agents who
have just emerged from Russia.


Like rats preparing TO abandon
sinking ships, the commissaries
keep airplanes, pilots. merchandising
and gasoline ready night and day
so they can escape from Petrograd
and Moscow by air the moment an
uprising begins. The pilots have
been promised huge rewards for
flying out of Russia when the smash
comes.


Talk of War Peril.


The aviation preparedness is ex-
planned to the people as being nee
essary, owing to the possibility of
war with Poland and RumanIa-


Many high bolshevist officials are
taking their wives and children to
Czecho- -Slovakia and the Baltic
states, carrying with them huge
amounts of platinum. gold, silk,
jewelry and foreign securities for
deposit in English and American
banks.


They pretend to be making ON
cial journeys. but few are return
ing to red Russia when once they
are outside, and none brings back
his family.


Peasants Burn Freight Cars,


Famishing peasants are tearing
up railway tracks and burning
freight cars whenever they are left
unprotected, in order to prevent the
conhscation of crops.


The soldiers who are kept mo-
bilized along the western frontier
on the pretext that Rumania and
Poland are preparing an attack are
muttering and breaking out, despite
the daily wholesale executions.

night attack, which took the navy

airplanes last night.


About nine O'Clock residents Of
Norfolk and its environs stared aloft

High above the dainty forms of four

houhetted against the luminous back

Calcium Flares.

with one accord the rour air wasps

ing rays of the flares.

ant chief Of the air service. who has

In the past month to demonstrate tho
efficiency and superiority OF airplanes

Last week fliers under the leader.
ship of General Mitchell bombed
