NEW YORK, Jan. 4.-The three
"lost" American balloonists came
home today. They arrived in spe-
cial train from Buffalo, n. Y, at
1896 o'clock this morning. Though
a drizzling rain had turned the snow
into slush and a mist hung over the
city, a good-sized crowd waited in
the street to greet the heroic trio.


300 At STATION.


As they aIighted from their train,
Lieutenants Kloor. Farrell and Hinton
were welcomed by some 300 persons,
including many women. Among these
were city officials. naval officers and
relatives and friends.


Mrs. stephen Farrell and Mrs.
Walter Hinton were at the station
nearly an hour before the train ar
rived. both bubbling over with JOY.
Tears glistened in many eyes when
the two licutenants who had come
back literally from the shadow OF
death by exposure and starvation in
the frozen wilds of the Northland
leaped from the train the. moment
it stopped and embraced and kissed
thier wives.


The fistic encounter at Mattice
and all the acrimony that surrounded
ed some phases OF the great ad-
venture seemed forgotten.
CROWDS GIVES CHEERS.
p As the three lieutenants accom-
panied by the men and women who
had welcomed them. passed through
the main hall of Pennsylvania sta
ton, the 500 odd persons scattered
there quickly grasped their Identity.
and there were many hearty cheers
and impromptu handshakes.


From the moment the train pulled
in until the three naval men and
the escorting group disappeared In
the Pennsylvania Hotel, which is
across the street from the station,
there was a steady click of dozen
cameras, while small army or
newspapermen surrounded the trio
and fired endless Volleys of aues-
tions at them.


RUSE OF AIRMEN FAILS.
A ruse by the three aeronauts to
evade the crowd that thronged the
station proper by taking q subway
passage to the hotel failed. for fully
500 persons rushed after them, cheer
ing. calling the names of the three
lieutenants over and over, and in



and shaking hands.


Miss Alexandra Flowerton. Lieuten-
ant Kloor's sweetheart, also was at
the station. She and the wives OF
Lieutenants Hinton and Farrell were
repeatedly in danger OF being crush
ed to death by the crowd that storm
ed and milled around the naval trio.
so dangerous did the rush become at
one time that photographers and
newspapermen formed n human bar
ricade between the three women and
the crowd, holding the impetuous
throng back with arms, sticks, and
camera stands.


Photographers had a trying time
endeavoring to take flashes of the
aeronauts and the three women. Just
when they thought they had things
fixed" for mice group picture
the crowd would storm forward again
and spoil IL.


Look into the camera" came the
constant beseeching cry OF the pho
tographers as they frsntically tried 10
get the focus"


Which camera" Lieutenant Farrell
kept saying, with a broad smile, sur
veying the array of apparatus lined
up in front. behind, and sideways OF
himself and his brother officers.


"Hurrah for Farrell" shouted a
woman. YES, hurrah for Farrell!"
Joined chorus of hundreds. But as
to prove that New Workers don't dis
criminate between the three heroes,
the throng promptly followed this
with cheers for the two other balloon
lists.


Thunderous cheers greeted the group
on their arrival in the Pennsylva MIA
Hotel lobby.

Sailormen are not noted for the
amount of cash they carry away from
port with them, but the crew Of the Zui-
bona. a freighter now 500 miles out.
bound for Trieste, scraped together
enough money yesterday to send wire
less back to New York.


The radio message. somewhat unln-
telligible, either because of static in the
atmosphere or emotion in the breasts of
the senders, announced that the crew
was through. irrevocably through, with
the line. Their wine had given out. A.
J. Bachman. marine superintendent of
Phelps Brothers, agents of the vessel
here, read the message without outward
dismay and then remarked that the line
was through, irrevocably through with
the crew.


They kicked while in port, he said,
because no place was provided to go
swimming save the cold bay, because
newspapers were delivered on board
daily and because the chef and baker
weren't fired for maltreating the grub.
Later when the ship got to sea they
kicked some more, and when she came
back after two days for minor repairs
they kicked even harder. Unable to get
wine here, the agents put on board $50
cases of near beer. but. judging from the
radio, the near beer has just been dis
covered to be the only thing on board
the Zuibona without kick.

bert

Sequence of any protest by the foreign
banks, President Zayas several days ago

uation. Should the newspapers disre-
gard the Governments request, the Sec
retary continued, such other methods as

taken TO protect Cuban financial institu-
/. items.

disposed to give them every guarantee.
without the necessity of presenting Tor
NAL complaint or adopting measures

tions, which it was reported the leading
hanks considered they might be impelled

the Government had initiated this cam
paign as result of the recent suspen-
sion of payment by several banks, Which.

rency to meet runs by depositors whose
confidence had been shaken through
newspaper stories on the banking situa-
ton.


Publicity which unjustly undermines

depostors not only is an offence against

crime against the entire nation, for bhtil
the financial system and the welfare OF
the republic are affected Senior Celia
bert declared. "and the Government has
voluntarily adopted efficient measures
to meet this evil with ut awaiting sug-
gestions or threats from outside
sources


Major-Gen. Enoch Fl. Crowder, repre-
senting the United States Government,
who had not conferred with President
Zayas since the Presidents inauguration
ON May 20, began series of conferences
with the Chief Executive this afternoon.

weeks.

gin, who had 10 seconds, in l minute

LOCKPORT, N. Y, April 3o.-Anna
E6son Taylor, the only woman who
ever navigated Niagara Falls in bar
rel and lived, died in the Niagara Coun-
ty Infirmary to-day.


Mrs Taylor made the trip over the
falls on October "a, 1901, in crudely
constructed wooden barrel as cast
at fortune, but i'll fortune pursued her
from the time of her adventure to the
time of her death. She was fifty-eight
years old.


Mrs. Taylor was towed out from La
Sale, two miles above the falls, by
river men into the Canadian channel,
so that her barrel would pass over the
Horseshoe Fall, where the water was
deepest.


Her barrel passed safely through the
upper rapids, made the plunge near
the middle of the Horseshoe. and re-
appeared in the spume below the falls
within half an hour. Mrs. Taylor was
severely injured and it was necessary
to cut the barrel in halves to get her
out. While she was receiving medical
attention her barrel was stolen.


She recovered from her injuries and
made lecture tour of the West, but
met with little success.

In front of the Cathedral of
Rheims has long stood the familiar
stone figure of Joan of Arc on horse
back, holding aloft broadsword.
In this same cathedral in 1929 the
Maid of France had taken part in
the coronation of Charles VII.


When the great war started the
Germans attacked Rheims and
dropped shells and bombs in and
about the cathedral. The roof was
destroyed, the wonderful carving
was shattered, the glorious stained
glass windows were broken into bits
and the church was all but ruined


Yet Joan of Arc sat unscathed on
her stone horse holding aloft her
sword. The bishops palace next
the cathedral was bombed. the
greater portion of the city was con-
sumed by fire, but Joan was un-
touched. The credulous among the
handful of inhabitants who pre-
ferred constant danger in their own
homes to safety and inconsistencies
back of the lines came to look upon
the statue of the Maid with new rev.
erence. Shells and bombs fell about
her, but Heaven protected her.


Then came March, 1918. The
morale of the world was low. Ger
man forces were breaking the Allied
lines and defeat was almost in sight.
Fearing that harm would finally
come, the statue was removed to a
place of safety. Rheims is doomed!"

Field Marshal Won Buelow's name
will always be associated with Ger
many's desperate effort to win the
World War in single campaign
an effort which broke down in the
First Battle of the Marine. He was
in command of the Second German
Army, which engaged, with the First
and Third armies, in the great turn
ing movement through Belgium.
During the greater part Of this
movement he was also in command
Of Won Kluck's First Army, which
held the extreme German right. The
development had been planned years
before by Count Schlieffen. 1t was
carried through without hitch in
its first stages, owing to a faulty
concentration and faulty maneuver-
ing on the part Of the French. 1t
fell to pieces when the German right
wing armies drew near Paris and
then swerved away from the capital
southeast toward the valley of the
upper Seine.


Won Kluck resented his subordina-
ton to Won Buelow and at the criti-
cal moment of the swing away from
Paris disregarded instructions from
the German General Staff. His too
rapid advance uncovered the German
right flank and rear to Manoury's
attack and made the strategic posi-
ton of the German armies exceed
ingly difficult. The Germans we're
beaten in the First Battle of the
Marine by their own blunders. Ton
Buelow couldn't hold his own against
Franchet dEsperey's Fifth French
Army. But Won Kluck's failure to
obey instructions had already made
inevitable the German check and the
retreat to the Aisne.


Won Buelow and Won Kluck have
fought out their differences at
length in their military memoirs.
Both were retired in 1915. They
had had their chance and missed it
more through Won Moltke's short
comings than their own. But few
soldiers ever had a greater chance.

The steamship West Hematite, from
Dunkirk. brought to port yesterday
three men and woman from Brooklyn,
who were picked up chilled and ex-
hausted in dory that was drifting sea-
ward off the Ambrose Channel Light
ship on Monday night.


John Javelon, the oldest of the party,
said the two men with him were his
brothers and the woman his wife. They
had gone out from South Brooklyn
Monday in motor boat and trailing a
dory.


The heavy gale which came up in the
afternoon caught and carried them sea-
ward. The heavy seas kicked up by
the wind swamped the motor boat and
it capsized. Realizing that such mis-
hap was inevitable, the Javelons had
got into the dory and cut adrift from
the launch before it sank.


Their cries were heard on the West
Hematite about midnight and they were
taken aboard. They said their home
was in Sixteenth Street. Brooklyn.

BRUSA, Asia Minor, Sept. 16 (By
The Associated Press s).-Crown Prince
George of Greece narrowly escaped
capture by mounted Turkish irregulars
while en- route to this city from the
battle front this week. The motor car
in which the Crown Prince, General
Stratigos and other officers were trav-
cling toward Eski-Shehr, was attacked
just after it had left the west bank of
the Sakara River. Turks opened fire
from hillside. The bullets came close
to the Prince, but the driver speeded
up the car and the party escaped.


This was the second close call the
Prince had within a fortnight. While
he was at general headquarters, at
Uzumbek, an attempt to capture him
was made by Turkish irregulars, who
evidently planned to make the whole
general staff prisoners. The attack
was frustrated, however, by machine
gun and rifle fire


Prince George has joined his father,
King Constantine, here.

time is often described as one worthy

said. indeed. that no better fortune
could befall the country than a re.
vival Of the respect that existed then

BALTIMORE. March 31.--James Cardi-

was buried to-day with all the honors

the largest assemblage OF church digni-
taries which ever met on the continent.

flock poured into the Cathedral OF the

able 10 press into the church. stood rev.
orently for three hours while the pontifi-
cal requiem mass was being sung.

Louis took the pulpit during the long

gized him as "the great leader and SOL

ioned educator, the great patriot, the
kindly. gentle old man." The service
ended shortly before / o'clock after the

When dusk came the body was lifted

days and placed in a simple coffin

bishop OF Baltimore Then the casket

tered the doors Il few minutes before 10

Berlin, July %.


German students held their second
national convention at Erlangen, where
they divided their time between dis.
cussing nationalism and the prospects
Of making q living. Just after the ar
mistice the universities were hothouses
of liberalism, which. however, nearly
died as result of the Treaty Of Yer.
sailles. Their professors attributed
German poverty and disorganization tc
the Allies rather than placing the re-
sponsibility on the proper shoulders
Despite the poverty which reduced the
monthly income of German students tc
Sc, they remained mostly conservative.


The delegates to the Erlangen conven-
ton made violent political speeches. The
real problem, however, was meeting the
hard times. Would the students sacri'
flee patriotism sufficiently to accept re.
lief from enemy countries? One zealot
induced the students of Magdeburg tc
abstain from making an appeal. When
they left, however, the university unan-
imously appealed to the Quaker relief
organization


Although caste and fraternity lines
are sharply drawn in German universi-
ties, poverty Is now forcing the students
to adopt more of community life They
are forming cooperative lunch rooms,
sanitariums and employment agencies.
Three thousand cases of consumption
show the effects of bad nourishment
among them. The students have become
shoemakers and bookbinders, and are
working part time at various trades.


Many of the students are learning a
trade while pursuing their studies, with
the hope Of earning living In the out
side world where learning is now the
cheapest commodity and Inducements to
scholars most limited. There are $500
unemployed teachers In Germany. and
half of those with positions are receiv-
ing less than living wages. The students
came to the convention in old clothes,
and many wore patched uniforms, show
ing how the present poverty has forced
them into admitting an equality which
they have always resisted.


After the Erlangen convention, Gen.
Ludendorff. In addressing the municipal
students, deplored the tendencies evinced
at the convention. I'VE must train the
men of Germany" he said, adding that If
the students failed there was small hope
for the nation. After the war veterans
who are now studying have be- grad
uated the quality of the German students
would be greatly lowered, he added.
and left no doubt that he looked pessi-
mistically into the future.

An army truck loaded with supplies
and manned by five men of the army
transport service plunged into the
water between two piers at the army
supply base at the foot Of Fifty eighth
Street, Brooklyn, yesterday afternoon.


Private Marianne Facceola, nineteen
years old, of Company No. 1, Army
Elizabeth Street. Manhattan, was
drowned. He was driving the truck
The four other men were rescued


The truck was coming from Hobo
ken with food supplies Tor the trans
ports Mansemond and American, which
are lying up at the foot of Fifty ighth
Street. Facceola was forced to make
a sharp turn to avoid another machine.
The army truck wheels struck the ce-
ment stringpiece, about foot high,
which is supposed to serve as guard
against such accidents. The machine
was under such headway that it leaped
the stringpiece and the outer sea wall
and went aboard a coal barge, from
which it rolled into the water between
the two piers.


With Facceola were four sergeants.
They were Charles Kingsley, nineteen
years old, of the mine planter whist
Ter; Frank Tillup, twenty eight years
old, of the mine planter Storey; owen
Rowe, thirty years old, of the mine
planter Todd, and John Hebel, of the
mine planter Harrison. Freight hand
lers from the transports threw ropes
to the men struggling in the water
Edward Wiman, civilian employee at
the army base, leaped in and dived
several times, finally grasping Fac
ceola by the hair and towing him to
the barge, where he vas lifted out by
others. Wiman then swan out and
dove for Hebel who was towed to
safety. By this time Wiman was
almost exhausted, but ne went back
and found Tillup floating among bits
of timber and other debris. Wiman
managed to get Tillup to the barge and
both men were dragged out of the
water


Rowe, the only man to jump as the
machine cleared the seawall, rose near
the barge and pulled himself aboard,
while Kingsley, who went into the
water with the machine. seized rope
which was thrown to him.


The men were taken to the base hos
pital, where Major Young, commanding
the medical detachment, vainly worked
over Facceola for two hours with a
pulmotor. The other men were able to
return to their duties last night.

sometimes die for their principles.
Antoine Basetic, editor Of the Voice of
Truth. an Austrian paper. persisted to-
day with five bullets through his head
and neck.


Two young men came upon him in a
real estate office and shot him down.
The murderers escaped, but the police
believe the killing was the elimination
Of a long standing international poll
tical dispute. Basetic had long assailed
the republican ambitions Of the
smaller Balkan states and other
neighbors Of Austria and had thereby
made a number OF enemies He
favored an Austrian overload for these
states and his relentless editorials
famed the hatred Of their former resi-.
dents. Basetic leaves a widow and
three small children.

CHICAGO, November 17.-Twenty-
five persons were injured. two OF them
probably fatally. this morning, when
two fve-car elevated trains, loop
bound from the West Side, were
wrecked in a rear-end collision at the
Crawford avenue station, on the Oak
Park line.


Three steel coaches were demol-
ished and several victims pinned be-
meath the wreckage- Firemen with
acetylene torches cut through the
twisted metal to reach them.


Cars Telescoped.


The first train was leaving the
Crawford avenue station when
speeding five-car. all-steel express
dashed out Of the fog and crashed
through the rear of the car ahead.
Two heavy steel cars were telescoped.
Most of the seriously injured were in
these coaches.


Three hundred passengers in other
cars were thrown to the floors and
showered with broken glass. Many
suffered minor cuts and bruises. but
were able to proceed on other trains
after receiving first aid.


The more seriously injured were re-
moved by firemen to nearby restau-
rant. where napkins were used for
emergency bandages while awaiting
the arrival of physicians and am
balances.


Two May Die.


Patrick Mcclure. a guard on the
first train, was pinned under the
wreckage for more than an hour. un-
til firemen obtained torches and cut
through the mass of twisted steel
plates and beams. He may die. Will
liam Griffin, who was riding on the
platform with Mcclure, suffered a
crushed leg and also may die.


officials of the elevated lines said
after an investigation. that the motor
man of the express failed to see the
first train because Of the dense fog
and mist.

The death list was the greatest

ished private dwellings and their

all wires having been cut. Sol.

adic disorders. One death was re-
ported from a night clash in which

military did not propose to be
caught mapping as in 1915. While

arations were made for quick mob
ilization.


The lack of Sim Fein activity in
the rural districts was regarded as
an ominous sign. British officials
admittedly were "jumpy." They de-
clared they expected trouble Sun.
day and Monday.

bomb in O'Connell street, in the
heart of the city, this afternoon.
Three soldiers and several civili-
ans, including three women. were
wounded. No arrests were made.

LOUISVILLE, Jan. 23.-Night riders
appeared for the first time in several
years in the Blue Grass region of
Kentucky. Saturday night and Sunday
morning a band of about twenty-five
mounted. armed ana masked men
made a twenty mile circle in Bath and
Fleming counties. warning farmers
and growers not to sell, haul or raise
any more tobacco under threats of
personal violence and destruction of
crops, barns and homes.


The band was first reported near
the county line of Fleming county,
where they called T. S. Robertson,
wealthy grower, from his bed about
1880 o'clock and threatened his life
ii he sold any more tobacco this season
or raised or leased land to raise any
next year.


The band. he said, was composed or
about thirty masked men, all carrying
shotguns or rifles. He was addressed
bv one of four men, who, he said, APP
proached him with their backs toward
him. The others remained about twenty
wards away and covered him with their
guns. After they had finished their
threats they forced him to face away
from the road and said that they would
send bullet through him IL he dared

The next report showed that the band.
or one of similar size. had advanced
about fifteen miles further into the
hurley district. Near Bethel, Bath
county. three farmers were aroused and
summoned to their doors They were
told that they must not sell or haul any

From this point, which marks the
furthest inroads of the night riders from

toward the point where they had en-
tered Bath county. crossed the line into
Fleming county and, near Sherbourne,
threatened the lives of two farmers
named Shields and Tomlin. who had
been hauling tobacco for other farmers.

called farmers out, made threats and
passed on. Altogether about fifteen fam
lilies were terrorized. At several places
shots we're fired, apparently to frighten
the growers. No damage was done.

ing preparations for defence of Upper
Silesia should the decision Of the Allies

luxuries.


The Chancellors hasty departure from
Berlin to Breslau last night shows that
there Is considerable anxiety in Demo-
cratic Government circles over the situa-
tion. The Berlin Socialists are openly
asking for protection from counter mill
tary organizations and are warning the
Government that revolt similar to the
Kapp insurrection is threatening. Gen.

are reported to be in Breslau.

armament of the German volunteer units

Silesia has embarrassed the German
Government, a high German official said
tonight to The New YORK HERALD cor
respondent.


I'VE are bound by the treaty to pre-
vent the Importation of arms and mill
tary formations" he said. but disarm-
ing Gen. Won Hoefer's forces would leave

coming Polish uprising which we know

THE NEW York HERALD correspondent
then sought allied officials and asked
how far the disarmament orders are
being executed. The French stated that
the Interallied Control Commission Is
there, but It hardly expects more than
formal satisfaction because the German
nationalist organizations continue re-
cruiting and existing formations are
maintained.


Gen. Won Hoefer's forces of irregulars
in Upper Silesia have more than fifty
suns, the Control Commission informed
the correspondent. Gen. Nollet, head OF
the Allied Commission. stated that the
German Government has made formal
fulfilment of the essential disarmament
demands, but the actual execution of
this programme would not be measur-
able until after the two months inven-
tory Is completed.


Orders Disregarded.


The Allied officials informed the cor
respondent that frequently the German
Governments orders are disregarded by
the subordinate officials. The disarna-
ment commission refused to have further
relations with the German disarmament
ministry after a long series of arrogant
letters and ignored requests and now all
business passes through the Foreign Of
flee. The terms OF Bavaria's submission
to the Allies demands involved the de-
livery Of some 100000 rifles and 2.7s0
machine guns, but the Allies have no
idea Of the quantity of arms still re-
naming.


The French are concerned almost ex-
clusively with the disarmament pro-
gramme while the British are concen-
trating their attention on Industrial
supervision. and are now taking the
initiative in the Transformation OF Ger
man war industries to peace uses.


Constant petty deceptions have now
led the Allies to a decision to continue
military control indefinitely. Allied Of
ficials say that they regard fears OF a
German military revival in the near fu-
ture as unfounded. but they add that the
present disarmament measures of the
Allies are absurd without including per-
manent industrial control, when the
German factories are capable of manu-
featuring thousands OF machine guns
daily.

slowed UP as far as new issues are con-

stagnant, but as yet there has been little

French absinthe distilers, whose

Only two distillers, Edward Premier
and Charles Henry. filed claims for
damages after the passage of the anti
absinthe act in 1915. Although they as
serted they had the same right to COM
pensation as had the growers of worm
wood, the courts followed the precedent
in the cases Of tobacco and match
manufacturers when the State took over
those monopolies. granting neither
manufacturer one centlme In damages
although their losses amounted to many
million francs.


In the case Of the absinthe makers.
their stills are said to be total loss,
as they cannot be used In connection
with any other chemical processes, while
the ahsinthe substitutes--new ones ap-
pearing every week at the Paris bars
can be concocted without the elaborate
apparatus required to make real alb
sinthe.
Incidentally. this may explain the fact
that the substitutes, which contain too
much paregoric for the American taste.
are rapidly supplanting beer as the
thirsty Parisians favorite tipple. and In
most cafes here they can be obtained
cheaper than the foaming book or amber.

To tho Editor of The Tribune.


Sir: Watch any city Pullman Office

ing for lower berths. I have known of
scores of cases where people wishing to
make some trip have given it up be-
cause they could get no space. They
unreasonably. assumed that they simply
couldn't sleep in an upper berth. Every
lower berth was sold and the railroad
naturally objected to putting on a
whole car for one or two lower fares
when most Of the upper berths were
still available.


Without losing q dollar the railroads
could cure this situation if they would
adjust prices so that instead Of being
one-ffth less, the upper were only one
half the price of the lower BERTH. e.,
raise the lower, and lower the upper.
People who want to economic would
then call for uppers; people who don't
care what they pay would still take
lowers and the car would fill up. Why
not try this sensible solution, which
will please both rich and poor?


OLD TRAVELLER.

Under Chariot Wheels.

test.

that the regular Saturday night show
Of the club was allowed to 20 on last
night because of the fact that the

management and the boxers.

by Michaels for sixty days, and Johnny

TROM data collected from every available source
r the United States Public Health Service has
= prepared and published plans and specihca-
tons for model sanitarum for tuberculosis patients,
especially those from the world Where possible
these plans will be followed in future service hospital
construction; and where conditions will allow
act adherence they will be used so far possible


The plans group the administrative buildings in
the center around three sides of open court. Fac
ing from fourth side, roadway, stands the
nhrmary, its wards radiatng away in wheel-spoke
fashion. On the opposite side of the administration
buildings, close up, is auditorium and open-ar
theater. short distance beyond this the wards for
semi-ambulant patients disposed along concave
arc; and little farther away the wards for the
ambulant patients. The officers. nurses and attend
ants quarters severally grouped here and there
the right; and the industrial buildings (power
house, etc.) grouped the left. Provision is
made for occupational therapy and for vocational
training for selected patients.


A concerted effort is being made by the United
States Public Health Service and the National Park
Service, to make the national parks of the United
States safe and sanitary for the vast numbers of
Americans who have recently taken to touring them.
Before the war, when tourists were fewer and most
of them travelled stage lines and stayed at park
hotels, the sanitary problem simple Since the
war, however, the great majority travel in automo-
bies and camp out, enormously complicating all
health matters. -


Since early in January the United States Public
Health Service the request OF and in cooperation
with the National Park Service has been preparing
for the work; and on May IS, it sent its first sani-
tary engineers into Yellowstone, Mount Rainier Yo-
semitic and Grand Canyoun parks. Other engineers,
engineers who have finished work their earlier
assignments, will go to other parks. Only in the
largest and most popular parks, such the Yellow
stone will it be necessary for sanitaran to remain
all summer.


The work consists in examination and protection
Of water supplies, disposal of garbage and sewage,
inspection of milk and food and the way they are
handled providing for camp policing and sanitation,
and prevention of malaria. Malaria carrying mosqui
toes have been found in Yosemite Park, and special
efforts will be made to eradicate them there and to
prevent them from acquiring residence" in other
parks.

The ocean-going tug Three Friends.


which attracted worldwide attention as


a hlibusterer prior to the outbreak of


the Spanish war as a result
of her exploits in transporting arms


and ammunition from the United States
to Cuba for the Cuban revolutionists,


has been purchased by local shipping
concern from the estate of the late Gov


ernor and United States Senator-elect
Napoleon b. Broward, who commanded


her during part of her adventurous
career, and will be converted into a


wrecking tug.


The Three Friends, built in Jackson


vile in 1895, is 112 feet in length and
although designed solely for towing pur-
poses her lines and power were such
that she easily could show her heels to
all but the speediest warcraft of the
day When gun running became popu-
lar and profitable she Joined the tug
Dauntless, commanded by the widely
known Dynamite Johnny" O'Brien, and,
successfully eluding numerous Spanish
and American warsnips sent to capture
them, the two vessels landed cargo after
cargo of munitions for the Cuban
patriots.


Other vessels also were engaged in
filibustering, but their activities soon
were overshadowed by the hair raising
! exploits of the Three Friends and the
Dauntless and the names of the two
| tugs became familiar throughout the
| world.

They had started their perilous task

hair.

wAvERLy, Mass. Aug. 19.--The most

foot putt. and George Duncan. with his
ball but seven feet from the pin. missed

combination lead In the morning round.

the defeat sustained by the former lis the
fourth they have thus far encountered,
two of the four coming when Greater
Boston golfers have paired with Hutchi-
son against the British team.

street area in Belfast this morning

held attended by officers of the police
and the military by leading towns
people to discuss the situation here in
view Of the disorders that had occur
red during the week. Acute trouble

York street and North Queen street
districts. several civilians being
wounded in fighting in which the po-
lice and the military were forced to
intervene. The rioting stopped alb
ruptly at the curfew hour. but it was
announced that reinforcement Of the
military in Belfast from adjoining
areas today was contemplated

rioting were made public this morn
ing it developed that two persons

only.


Four years later the democratic party
made a shift, and put the financial
question above the tariff question, and
the young man from the west became
the party's leader. takign the honor
in circumstances of dramatic intensity
at the party's national convention.


The young man from the east bolted

country against the candidate: and

ed They have not been in agreement
since, though both have remained
democrats. Last year they met as
delegates at San Francisco, the man

vets, the man from the west the cham

building on Capitol Hill the other day.
the one-again member Of the
House-chattng with friends in the
chamber, the other entertaining a
knot of admirers in one of the cor
ridors. They are no longer young,

age. The figures of both have filled
out The one has lost much of his
hair, but what remains retains it's
youthful color. The hair Of the other

Upon the whole, time has dealt
kindly with both w. Bourke Cochran
and William j. Bryan.

husband testified.

thur Carr, one of the prisoners. who

State Police Headquarters here received
reports tonight that West Virginia
State trooper and Kentucky National
Guardsman were killed at Nolan, west

battle zone was resumed.

tain j. R. Brockus, the latter said.

George Crum, civilian, was wounded,
the advices said,

ceived, State police officials ordered
the Norfolk & Western Railroad Com
pany to prepare a special train for an
Immediate run to Nolan.


Nolan is located on the West Vir-
ginia-K Kentucky border, on the Tug
River, opposite the line which divides
Pike and Martin counties, Kentucky.

from Norton indicated that two men,
Victor Elkins and Clyde Harper, had
been arrested in connection with the
fight. They were charged with carry
ing arms, the captain said.

Mr.. Milani, the representative of

and German firms or their agents
more numerous than American, but
also they are more fully expert
enced in the needs of that market;
for which reason the Argentine buyer
is more likely to deal with them.


Long ago it was remarked, with
much truth, that American CONNER
cial agents went to South America
with full sample cases, while Euro
speans went with theirs empty. The
Americans carried samples Of the
goods which were made in the
United States to suit the tastes and
needs Of the people of the United
States and tried to persuade South
Americans that those were the
goods which they ought to use, fire.
quently with negative result. The
Europeans filled their empty cases
with samples of the goods which the
South Americans were using and
which they wanted to keep on using,
took them home to Europe and had
factories there turn out precisely
such goods, purely for the South
American trade.


When one salesman tries to sell
folks things that they don't want,
on the ground that he knows what
they ought to want better than they
do themselves, and another offers
them the things that they do want,
there can be little doubt as to which
will be the winner.

THERE was once good old farmer and hi.


wife, in the State of Minnesota, who had been
pioneers together. They had worked and saved
until they had reached the time when they had a
surplus in bank and decided to invest it on the
farm. He wanted barn to replace the patch
work affair which was the original stable with ad
dtons. She wanted house. where there
would be comfort and convenience, with measure
of beauty He with the simple argument that
the barn would build the house for her, but
the house could never build the barn for him.


This same process of the logic of economics is
guiding the restoration OF North France. I The
work OF restoration began in the fields They were
reclaimed from the runous effects of shell fire and
made fit for cultivation. Next have come barns for
the stock and pens for the chickens. Last is to
come the farm homes. 1t is natural that the
French famous for their genuine thrift, should
adopt this policy. Yet it has been common in this
country.


The Pennsylvania Dutch were known for their
big red barns and modest dwellings. This example
spread and all through the countrys farm districts
it will be found that the barns have built the
more pretentious modern farm homes. No better
indication of the swift revival of North France
could come than this decision of the French to
earn before they spend themselves.


The early Scandinavians who came to the North
west States often lived in dugouts in hillsides, in
caves like the Trogodites until their labor their
fields and cattle earned home for them.


The has not spoiled the French. Their sac
rihces for their country have not given them the
false belief that their country owes them
life of ease. Sacrifice is but badge of nobility,
not of ideness nor clearinghouse ticket 1t
but test6es that what man can do for his country
or for others he do for himself. Sacrifice with
pay is not sacrifice; but genuine sacrifice shows
exactly the quality the French showing in
building for themselves the devastated regions
first the CROP then the barn and last, comfort for
themselves.

DUBLIN, Feb. 25.-One of the big
gest battles in the warfare which has
been raging in Ireland was fought
today near Ballyvourney when the
crown forces were defeated by a
heavy section of the Irish Republican
Army.


1t is known that two members of
the crown forces were killed and
upwards OF six wounded, but the
total casualties have not been
checked up.


Belief was expressed that the cead
may number ten The Sim Fein
casualties were said to have been
heavy. In the Macroom district Brit
ish troops and military policemen
have trained As machine guns upon
the roads to prevent ambuscades.


At o'clock the known dead num-
bered four.


Hundreds of English soldiers were
rushed to the Ballyvourney district.
A military airplane hovered over the
scene throughout the afternoon, scout
ing for bands of armed men.


One of the dead was Major Grant,
commanding the Black and Tan police.


There were more than 800 Sim
Feiners in the band which attacked
the military police.


Eight police Iorries filled with
Black and Tans were passing through
the Coolea District, west of Macroom
when they ran into roads that had
been mined.


An attack was opened upon the lor-
ries with the Sim Feiners firing from
behind barricades.


From a skirmish the engagement
grew into a furious battle with the
crash of gunfire audible for miles.
Reinforcements of heavy armed
policemen were rushed to the scene from
the Cork barracks and Joined in the
fray.


The roads in the Ballyvourney dis
trict are fianked with wooded hills,
affording excellent shelter for at
tackers.


1t was understood there were about
seventy black and tan policemen in
the lorries that were attacked.


According to information received
here this afternoon the crown forces
being outnumbered, were compelled
to retreat after an action of two
hours, leaving part of their wounded
behind them on the battlefield.


LONDON, Feb. 25.-The comman-
dant of a detachment of police cadets
and several policemen were killed
when 100 Sim Feiners ambushed the
cadets near Ballyvourney today. said
a Central News dispatch from Dublin.

PITTSBURGH, Dec. Boa bed
ridden invalid for five years, Mrs.
Martha Wuchenich, forty-two years
old. yesterday crawled on her hands
and knees to a fire which had
started in her bedroom and with her
hands beat out the flames, saving her
own life and preventing destruction
Of her home.


Aroused by her calls, George Wuch-
enich, the husband, came to the aid Of
mis- stricken wife, but not until several
minutes after she had practically
extinguished the fire. Mrs. Wuch-
enich was burned about the hands,
but not seriously injured.


The invalid was awakened by
smoke and, crawling and rolling from
her bed, she worked her way slowly
to the side Of the room where the
wallpaper was ablaze and the fire
spreading rapidly.


Working frantically, despite her in
firmities, she beat the flames down SO
that only a few small pieces of paper
were aflame on the room floor when
her husband reached the scene.

Statesmen for mems clothing manu-

from their initial fall selling trips
report fair business throughout the
country, except in the South and the
other strictly agricultural sections.

been placed cautiously, according to

have been unable to make any esti-

freedom, although few retailers have
contracts for more than so per cent of
their estimated requirements. The
average is nearly 40 per cent, &C.

Conductor Leopold Stokowski. with
the Philadelphia Orchestra, yesterday
afternoon. at the National Theater,
carried his large and distinguished
depths of musical composition and in
depreciation. With his soloist, Nine.
Yelanda Nero. the Hungarian pianist,
something very near an ovation was
registered, while with the remarkable
and most unusual Schoenberg COM
positions, which have been laughed at,
Missed and almost jeered off the con-
cert stage, he had an appraisal in
perhaps every form in which an audi
ence can express its feelings.


Nine. Mero's triumph was scored
with Liszts Concerto in A Major" for
piano and orchestra. and Washington
has seldom, If ever,e had so rare, so
treat. The applause that rang from
all parts Of the house was spontane-
Gus and almost overwhelming, recall
ing the artist again and again. Nine.
Mero's artistry Is little short of phe-
nomenal and with the splendid sup
port OF the orchestra seemed fully SO.
She has the power of lion and the
gentle touch of fairy, while her
wonderful fingers pass from a thun-
dering fortissimo in the bass to the
utmost delicacy and dexterity required
for almost lightning-like runs. She
:" iAS lTOHl tHc pldHO us sweetest anu
it's grandest tones with equal facility
and skill. Her performance was rare
and beautiful artistry.


Mr.. Stokowski modestly explained
the difficulties he had encountered
with the Schoenberg compositions.
He said he had made a study Of them
for nine years. often turning his back
upon them. even for a year, only to
return, until he had reached the con-
clusiDn that the man who wrote them
must be genius. He did not object
to the audience showing it's real feel
ing concerning them. but urged only
that they be given an attentive hear
ing. Some day, maybe. Washington
will understand and appreciate them,
but not soon.


But the delighted astonishment at
Nine. Mero's performance and the
amazement at Schoenberg's give
Orchestra Pieces" that seemed much
to the unlearned like a nightmare of
disintegrated jazz music. did not
overshadow the wonderful beauty of
Wagner's prelude to Lohengrin," the
opening number, nor the dainty and
delicious rendition of Debussy's s
prelude a lapres-midi dun faune.'
nor the majestic grandeur of Sibelius'
tone poem. "Finlandia," which closed
the concert. 1t was novel and
glorious afternoon for music lovers.


The next, or third. concert of the
Philadelphia Orchestra will be given
January 10, when the distinguished
guest conductor. Vincent D'Indy, will
direct. Mr.. Stokowski probably will
not appear again this season.

three years ago tomorrow morning

Captain Giuseppe Schiafino and
twenty-nine men of the Italian
freighter Alacrita, which foundered in
hurricane at sea nine days ago,
reached New York yesterday on board
the Spanish cargo ship Cabo Cruex.
They had been trying to reach the
coast in an open boat without drinking
water or supplies.


The Alacrita foundered September
16, when sudden hurricane caught her
broadside and unshipped her rudder.
The ship was thrown on her beam ends
and with a shifted cargo was unable to
right herself. With a heavy list to
starboard, she lay exposed to the
tremendous sea which tore off her
matches and flooded the hold. The
cargo of loose grain became saturated
and efforts to pump the water out
were vain. Captain Schiaffino and his
crew kept the pumps going eight hours,
at the end of which time the storm
abated, but the ship was sinking
stern first and on the morning of Sep
tembcr II was abandoned. Ten
minutes after being deserted, the
Alacrita sank


Several of Crew Delirious


Captain Schiaflino divided his crew
into watches and kept the two boats
under way in a heavy sea that fire.
quently filled them to the gunwalcs
and necess ssitated constant bailing. The
crew were insufficiently clad and suf-
fcred severely from exposure. When
F,11 I, ,<.l,% Iox,
light on September 81, six men were
unconscious and several were delirious.


The Alacrita's home port was Savanna,
Italy. Sho was built twenty-seven
years ago, was 320 feet long and regis
tered 4,5OO tons. The ship was bound
for New Orleans when she left Italy
and made that port in safety, unload
ing and shipping a cargo for Norfolk.
She left Norfolk September 8 with
cargo of grain for Spain. When the
storm struck, the ship was fifty-fve
miles off Bermuda. Captain Schiaffino
tried to head into the wind but was
caught before he could bring the ship
about. With steering gear disabled
efforts were made to rig jury rud-
der, but without success.


When the boats were lowered, be-
cause of danger that they would be
pounded to bits against the ships side,
it was necessary to hold them off fifty
yards, compelling the ships crew to
dive overheard and swim to the boats
All were picked up.


When the rescue ship docked in
Brooklyn last night officers of the
Italian immigration Society took charge
of the Alacrita's crew. More than half
the men were in state of collapse. All
were destitute Of clothing, except for
OllSkinS and deck ClOthinp thew had
worn when overtaken by the storm.
The crew will be housed for the pres
ent at Italian immigration headquar-
ters, Water Street Captain Schiaf-
fino and his staff of officers remained
on board the Cabo Creux.


The rescue took place in latitude
1904 north and longitude 5534 west.
The crew had covered more than sixty
miles in their boats when picked up.

TERRE HAUTE. Dec. 29.-Eugene
v. Debs was welcomed home last night

$1,000 men. women, and children. the
home folks Of Terre Haute and the

Twenty-six years ago Debs was

UP their cameras, but were swept OH
their feet. Police were helpless to hold
back the throng3.

torches. He kissed his hand to the
cheering crowds as they streamed
along behind bearing white placards
on which various legends were In

1.-THE Great Humanitarian, He

A band led by two men carrying
o long streamer with the words, wei

crowded streets to the Debs home, an

building line to building line OF the

Mrs, Katherine Debs-Kate Debs,
Terre Hauters call her-stood silently.
,r1mly on the wide veranda. During
her husbands absence she has lived
alone in the old home with her aged
mother, Mrs. Katherine Baur, now
almost blind.


Mrs. Baur's prayer has been that she
might live long enough to see Gene
come home" When told that he had
stopped over in Washington and would

10 washingto he must be right. Gene
ie always right"


Wife In iii Health.


Mrs. Debs has suffered from heart
trouble, and II il feared the shock
OF the Homecoming might prove too
much for her. She expected her hus-
land on Thanksgiving. and then Tor
Christmas dinner. and recently rela-
tives had attempted to keep the news
from her until 1t was definitely as.
sured when Debs would be home. Blu,
c. few days ago she went shopping
and heard from others in the store
that he was coming.


As the torch-lit truck paused In front
OF her home, a band played Home,
Sweet Home" Debs, standing bare
headed, and Mrs. Debs, waiting at the
head of the steps, supported by her
brother, Arthur Baur and Mayor

He flung his arms around her. kissed

cheek as she buried hers upon his
shoulder. Thus they stood for a full
moment as tears streamed down their

After a brief speech from his front

The Chinese New Year was cele-
brated in Chinatown yesterday by
forty Japanese moving picture folk, a
half-dozen American screen actresses
and camera grinders and some Italian
bands and hurdy-gurdy players.


The moving picture outfit arrived
first. They came down to grind out a
good old Chinese melodrama and
thought they might as we'll take ad-
vantage of the Oriental street deco
rations with which the Chinese might
be expected to usher in the year 1903.
This was their first delusion. The only
decorations were a few American flags
and a Chinese flag on Doyers Street,
near the midnight mission. The cam
eias were set up facing that.


The second deltssion was that the
Chinese, like American film fans, could
be expected to mistake Japanese for
Chinese. This delusion was shattered,
along with some empty milk bottles, as
soon as the japanese, In Chinese cos
tunes, were seen violently pulling the
white actresses into dark Railways,
flashing daggers and generally acting
the way the Chinese are supposed to do
in pictures and on the stage. 1t took
the American Chinese of Chinatown five
minutes to put the Japanese Chinese to
rout toward williamsburg Bridge, using
American milk bottles.


The Italian musicians succeeded the
japanese in Chinatown. They played
on street corners and collected nickels
from American sightseeing buses,
whose Chinese lanterns gave the sec
tion Mongolian touch.


Yesterday, the residents of China
town settled their debts as usual on
New Years, exchanged cards, closed
stores and played games, but dragged
no paper dragon through the streets
as of yore.


The Chinese residents were all in
their meeting halls, quietly playing
games, and the streets were darker
than usual. Early last night the only
people on the streets were 400 Ameri-
cans out of work, waiting to enter the
mission hall where the unemployed
sleep.

service to the Nation was rendered.


Lowered flags on public buildings,

wardly the Nations grief.

Matthews Church when the hour Of

resenting a Government in mourning

friends. The uniforms of Major General
March, Chief of Staff, and the officers

army. and Admiral Coontz, chief of
operations Of the navy and his officers,
marked high lights among the somber
black of the civilians.


When all were in their places. the
doors were opened to the throng that
waited outside and the church was
quickly filled.


Requiem mass was celebrated by
Monsignor Lee. rector of the church
which Justice White attended. AT the

zano, Papal Delegate, but there was no

puted region and conversations with all

where the Pilgrim Fathers laid the cor

initial presentation of the striking pag-

celebration.


A cast OIL more than 1900 men, women

Grated in the play. A distinguished

whcreon the pageant was enacted, two
interesting vessels strained at their
anchors. One was replica of the
Mayfower and the other was a replica
of Viking ship. Tonight was Gov
ernors night. Governor Charming Cox
and a number of Mayors of Massachu-
sets cities were among those who
keenly followed the pageant from it's
first scene to its brilliant finale. With
the possible exception of President
Harding's visit on August l, to-night's

preme Importance in connection with

merely because of it's rapidly changing

theme that was sustained throughout
the performance.

which pronounced the prologue, and
also came through the darkness at
dramatic moments during the play.

sodes divided into twenty seems and
firal. 1t first shows the coming to
America Of the Noisemen and the

plain, Admiral Biloxi, Captain John
Smith, Thomas Hunt and Captain
Thomas Dormer, before turning to the
life Of the Pilgrims in England and in
Holland. Then is shown the Pill
grims' voyage to Plymouth. The finale

little band made to present American

States early next fall.

decorated with the national colors.

expected

mouth Later he will occupy a box
at the ton of the mammoth semi

erims. will act the roles which their
forebears had in the settlement of

NOGALES, Ariz.. May 3.-The 25th
Infantry, Col. Carnahan, commanding,
last night was ordered held in readiness
for immediate action, when disorders
broke out in Nogales. Sonora, across the
international boundary. Army officials
said the move was precautionary, to
prevent shots being fired across the
line.


The trouble yesterday was precipi-
tated by the arrival at Nogales of
seventy-six Chinese and two Hindu la
borers from Hongkong. China, officials
stated. The foreigners were being ship
ped in bond from San Francisco


Five Chinese were badly hurt, three
of whom may die. physician attending
them at the Nogales hospital announced.


Acting American Consular Agent
Charles Daugherty said that the situa-
ton was well in hand.

man was staggering blindly and run

proved his worth against one of the
greatest runners of the world, was the
center of interest after his great race.
ne waited for Seagrove to recover, and

Vanquished as there was for the victor.

: HELSINGFORS. Finland, October

opened 120 kitchens and inspected no
less than 100000 children. With the
aid of thirty-ffve German doctors who
arrived there recently the American re-
lief unit is dividing the children into
three categories: First, those suffering
from illness and demanding immediate
attention; second, those suffering only
from malnutrition, and third, those able
to get along few weeks longer with
out relief.


Thirty thousand little ones have been
placed in the first category and are re-
ceiving regular rations. A bakery was
white rolls daily. Under the system
now in operation the children must
report to the kitchens in their dis
tricts and eat the food on the spot
none being allowed to carry provi-
sions home for distribution among
adults


Enough food has already arrived in
Petrograd to supply regular rations
to $4,000 children for three months
There is temporary stoppage in the
supply. but long before the reserve
is exhausted other shipments will ar
rive and enable the feeding of the
children to continue. The Pravada
praises highly the energy and ability
OF the American organization.

and Chicago, according to The Associ-
ated Press.

the Zeppelin Airship Building Com
pany, Of Friedrichshaven, and gave
their names as Harry Vissering and f..

conference with Weather Bureau OFF
cials here and in other cities. While

shrouded in secrecy, it is learned that

ply between Germany and America.

phere delicate recording instruments.

Special Despatch to THE NEW York HERALD.


PHILADELPHIA, July 24.-Twenty-two
men, fourteen white and eight negroes,
using two large automobile trucks and
two touring cars, early to-day stole $780,
900 worth of choice wines and liquors
from the warehouse of Norris Schiff.


SO well planned was the theft and so
successfully was it executed that the
police are without a clue to the crimi-
nails. The efficiency and speed with
which the barrels and cases containing
the liquors were transferred from the
warehouse to the trucks indicated that
the ground had been carefully gone over
before the raid was attempted. Even
the time had been selected with the ut
most care. Schig had left three hours
earlier for Atlantic City.


About 4 80 a. NJ. the men drove up
to the warehouse, which is in the rear of
Schifrs saloon. All the white men dis
tributed themselves as guards while the
negroes did the stevedore work. The
two touring cars were stationed at
startegic points to sound danger warn
ings.


The first step taken by the thieves was
TO remove the danger of any one calling
for the police. While the bandits were
engaged in binding and gagglng a watch
man and q baker in adjoining build
ings the negroes had broken down the
front door of the warehouse with a crow
bar.


Within thirty minutes the forty-five
cases and thirty-five barrels had been
transferred from the warehouse to the
trucks.


While this work was being performed
with such efficiency the fourteen white
men as guards had their hands full.
The noise made in breaking the doors
and rolling the liquor had awakened
many persons. Before the robbery had
been completed the police estimate that
there were at least one hundred watch
ing the operation. And yet so completely
did the handful of men have them cowed
that not one dared lead rush. Nor did
any of the spectators call the police.
Three families from houses Immediately
in the rear of the warehouse were locked
In q room.


Joseph Florlkowski. who is a competi-
tor of Schiff on the corner opposite
Schiffs place. watched the whole pro-
ceedings without sending in a warning.
After the booty had been loaded on the
trucks, he said n perfect military convoy
was formed. The first automobile, n
which were seven or the men, armed,
led the trucks by about one hundred
yards, while the other touring car fol-
lowed in their wake as a rear guard.
The saloonist followed the trucks several
blocks, but was soon left behind and lost
sight of them.


IL was not until half hour after the
robbers had made their getaway that
the police were notified.

CHICAGO, Nov. Is (Associated Press -
The United States Railroad Labor Board
announced tonight that new working
rules for the six shopcrafts probably
will be completed and issued in time to
become effective December /.


Issuance of the rules under recent
decision of the board paves the way for
consideration of requests which may be
filed by the roads for revision of the
shopcraft wage schedules


The new shopcraft rules will affect
approximately 500, 900 men on all Glass
l railroads in the country. Only ninety
four railroads are directly concerned in
the present case, the others not having
their submissions in proper shape when
the case was taken up, but board men,
bers anticipate that all the Class / rail-
roads will probably carry out the de-
cision without further hearings. The
boards statement issued tonight said :


''Such satisfactory progress during the
last week has been made in the consid-
Grafton of rules and working conditions
for the six shopcrafts that it is alto
gether probable these rules will be
completed and will become effective De-
cember L.


Five Months Consideration.


The board members said tonight that
the new rules have been practically COM
pleted in less than five months. while
the national agreement, which they
supersede, required the attention Of rail-
way, Government and labor representa-





fore 1t was completed.


The labor boa rd 5 work on the rules
was interrupted by the threatened rail-
road strike, which was averted October
27. A few days previously the board
had announced that no further wage
reductions for any class of employees
would be considered by the board until
working rules and agreements in dis
pute for that class of employees had
been passed on.


The board, it was indicated tonight.
will next take up for consideration the
rules and working conditions for the
maintenance of way employees. There
are a large number of disputed ques-
tions regarding these rules already be-
fore the board and statisticians have
prepared most of the cases for presen-
tation.





The national agreement which the
new rules will displace was first
brought before the Railroad Adminis-
tration in January, 1919. 1t was sub
mitted to a committee of twenty-eight
men, fourteen representing the em-
ployees and fourteen the roads. This
committee considered the rules for four
months, after which the findings were
reviewed by the National Board on Rail-
way Wages and Working Conditions.
The Railway Administration then
passed on the rules.


Steps for revision of the national
agreements before the labor board were
taken April 16 1920, after the railroads
and their employees had finished pre-
lminary negotiations both as to wages
and rules and working conditions with
out reaching, any agreement. The board
FASTENED the decision by ordering fur
ther conferences between employees
and the roads on rules and working
conditions. The results were reported
back to the roads, which in July began
the work of formulating new rules.

Bright and beautiful Venus is not

cur earth than any other OF the seven
planets-some twenty-six millions OF
n.iles-although at such a time she is
invisible. being hen between our world

BREMEN, Aug. 20.-Her former Ger
man crew and their families and
many Bremen Germans crowded this
port this week to view the steamship
George Washington, formerly the
North German Lloyd Companys larg-
est ship and which now flies the
American flag. The George Washing
ton arrived here on August 13 and
steamed from this port last Wednes-
day for New York by way of South
ampton.


During the whole of her stay here,
the piers were packed with Germans
watching the preparations for the
steaming for America of this big
first trip to Bremen since the begin
ming Of the world war, and on enter
ing port, as she steamed past the
crowds which lined the piers for miles,
there was an outburst of singing of
Deutschland Uber Allies and mad
cheering and waving of hands and
handkerchiefs.


The enthusiasm was explained as due
partly to old sentiment and partly be-
cause each ship arrival here means much
business for neighboring towns.


Most of Bremen Joyful.


THE NEW York HERALD correspondent
here asked an old German why he did
not celebrate. He answered that 1t was
because the ship was now under a for
eign and enemy flag. But the Bremen
population is joyful because their port
has again become a world harbor. and
this 10y exceeds chauvinistic hatred.
America is generally liked here and dol
lars are welcome.


The German designer of the vessel, an
aged and gray haired man. revisited the
ship this week and expressed his appre-
citation of the luxurious American fit
tings. However, he declared that the
present upkeep of the vessel was infe-
rior to that under the old German mer-
chant marine discipline.


American engineers aboard the George
Washington asserted that the vessel had
such a fascination for members of her
old German crew that It was necessary
to keep the engine room locked to pre-
vent them from overrunning It,


The collaboration of the United States
Mail Company with the North German
Lloyd seems to be effective and without
friction. The North German Lloyd
affords the American company docking
facilities here, at the same time handling
Ats entire passenger service in Bremen.
Ship cooks and stewards are recruited
largely In German ports and one-timc
German captain is now serving as pilot.
Bremen is again hummng with business,
I'D.
hotels being crowded with tourists.
American cotton merchants and other
business men have taken Offices here.


Anxious Over Receivership.


The North German Lloyd IS anxious
regarding the stability Of it's future re-
lations with tho United States Mail
Company. owing to the receivership OF
the latter concern and the Harri imam ne
gotiations over the line. THE New YoRz
HERALD correspondent here talked with
Herr Stinning. director of the North
German Lloyd, and other high officials
OF that company. They were convinced
that Hartman control would mean the
eclipse OF Bremen by Hamburg. because
tire steamships now running to Bremen
in the American service would be
switched to Hamburg. This situation
has develored a competitive tension be-
tween these two German ports. The
North German Lloyd people were re-
leved at hearing of the recevership i'm
stead of a transfer Of the United States
Mail, and tho probable outcome is that
they will be dependent on the United
States Mail Company, because they have
only seven small ships.


Herr Shining said that should its
United States Mail contract terminate.
the North German Lloyd was prepared
to begin limited service Immediately
and to enlarge 1t somewhat for the forth
coming tourist season. officials Of the
North German Lloyd avoided mentioning
1t, but It was said In well informed cir
cles that they had purchased six ships
from the British, with an average OF
5000 tons each, and now have ships
building OF between 10000 and 10000
tons

The Senate put through the House
resolution for general repeal of war
time laws last night and sent the
measure to conference. With few ex-
ceptions all of these laws, giving un-
usual powers to the executive, are to
be repealed under the bill. The ex-
ceptions include the trading with the
enemy act, the liberty bond acts and
the act creating the War Finance Cor
poration.


Among the laws which the legisla-
ton would repeal are the Lever food
and fuel acts, parts of which were
declared unconstitutional yesterday
by the Supreme Court. The Senate
judiciary committee had recommend
ed that the Lever law stand, but the
Senate adopted an amendment by
Senator Reed. democrat. Mo-. includ-
ing the food and fuel law among
those to be repealed.


The Senate also adopted a resolu-
ton by Senator Walsh, democrat.
Montana, providing that prosecutions
brought under laws which the resolu-
ton would repeal should not be af-
fected by the repeal.


In addition to the trading with-t the
enemy, liberty bond and other laws
which are exempted from repeal, the
resolution would restore the original
espionage act of 1917, repeating the
amendatory statute of 1913. The lat
ter was regarded as much more
stringent than the original act.
Another provision of the resolution
declares that it shall not operate to
prevent prosecutions Of Army and
Navy deserters or persons charged
with violating the selective service
law.

LEIPsIc, Sept. 2.-More than 100000
persons visited the Leipsic Fair DUR
ing the first few days it was open. The
displays are most comprehensive, there
being exhibited everything from farm
tractors to pins.


Apparently all German roads lead to
Leipsic now. For miles in every di-
rection signposts point the way to the
fair. and within the city at every turn
one comes face to face with placards
and signposts indicating the way to
the exhibition.


Viewed as a whole, the fair strik-
ingly accentuates the rapid develop
ment of great trusts in Germany, not
only among similar Industries but in
the bringing under one control in
dustries which are, in the kind of
goods manufactured, widely disso-
ciated. At the same time new inven-
tons and the wide range of manu-
featured articles shown indicates the
inherent vigor of German industry.


The chief aim Of the fair is to supply
the demand OF the home and European
markets for cheap goods However,
peace time quality is restored in most
of the goods shown. and the last trace
Of paper and leather imitation textiles
and rubber is disappearing.


The Krupps' Display.


The displays by the trusts are most
impressive. The Krupps have their own
building. which shows the transforma-
ton Of their factories from war time to
peace time production. The range Of the
Krupp output extends all the way from
needles to railroad locomotives. They
show a remarkable gravel car which can
be loaded by one man and which has
overhanging, bulging sides which make
It possible for double the ordinary load
to be placed aboard it.


The first Krupp cash register, the
study of which began year ago, rs
shown. Since American firms have OBJ
tanned authorization to import Amer
lean cash registers into Germany and to
manufacture cash registers here for sale
on the Continent the Krupps are push
ing production to win place in the
European market before the Americans
can develop theirs.


The Krupps have joined with the inn
portant optical firm of Ernemann in
Dresden for the manufacture and sale
of motion picture machines, and one of
their machines won a gold medal at an
exhibition in London recently.


The Krupps are also making non
unstable steel which differs from Eng
lish and Norwegian non-rustable steel
in that 1t possesses full cutting hard
ness. At the same time the firm is man
ufacturing gun parts. knives. medical
instruments and ordinary steel They
are even making steel for dental fill-
ings and bridge work, asserting it Is
more durable and more adaptable than
gold.


Arms Plant Makes Beds.


Another German trust engaging in an
even wider range of manufacture is the
Deutsche Werke, formerly Govern
ment arms plant and shipbuilding yard.
1t has eight factories, and Is now trans
formed into stock company which will
manufacture anything to meet a popular
demand. 1t displays ships, ship fittings,
ONCE furniture. kitchen utensils. iron
beds, lead solder and even artificial
hands. The prices of its goods are ex-
tremely low. owing to large scale pro-
duction and simple models. The Govern
ment Is still the largest stakeholder in
this concern.


One OF the most remarkable trust con-
centrations shown here Is that of Bing
Brothers, of Nuremburg. They have in
operation steel works and plants for the
manufacture of porcelain, jewelry, cut
lery, household wares and furniture, in
all twenty factories. Their display
shows such a wide range OF goods that
1t occupies an entire building.


This rapid extension Of the system of
trusts here Is enabling manufacturers
to reduce overhead expenses and meet
the new taxation demands.


Government Supervising.


A prominent customs official said the
Government was generally facilitating
expectation, but within certain limita-
lions. While German firms quote prices
considerably below foreign market
prices, the Government insists that
prices be increased with view to avoid
the accusation that Germany is dump
ing cheap goods and also to increase
home profits. The Government is also
hindering the expectation OF goods that

But the Chesapeake Beach Kid'

change her clothes. Year after year

long stockings, same black slippers.
same everything.


Now the kid" may have been

clothes were discarded with such
speed that the Chesapeake Beach

vinced that II was time to bounce

ash can.

had only thrown some Of her clothes

but she was too modest for modern
ideas of style. and into the discard
she went.


There were a few tears, of course.
but these dried quickly when the
mayor presented her successor, The
Chesapeake Beach Baby of 1921"
Oldest Inhabitants, men with long
white whiskers and stopped backs,
Strengthened right up and took a
new lease on life when they spied
her.


She's some baby. this 1921 girl

She wears a pair of trunks and q
sleeveless, low-necked shirt with a
pair of sport shoes for artistic ef-
feet alone. She wears no stockings
and she. looks half a century ahead

1891" will make her bow to the peo-
pie Of Washington this week. when

LONDON, Feb. 3.--The Irish Repub-

than FIVE hundred Sim Feiners, said
to have mobilized for an attack on the
+ olice barracks at Ross Carbery, am
bushed the police from comman-
deered house on the roadside.


The Black and Tans, numbering only
about twenty, were proceeding down
the road near Burgatia when overtaken.
They sought cover on the roadside,
fighting off their assailants until police
and military reinforcements could ar
rive. The crown forces finally sue
ceeded in routing the Republicans. kill
ing six of them and. wounding several,
although the exact number could not
be learned because the Sinn Feiners
carried their dead and wounded away
from the scene of the battle. The
Republicans left their arms and am-
munition behind in their flight. The
police had no casualties.


This is the largest concentration of

lorry in O'Conneil Street, and the other

ulary, who was shot down while cycling

mufti when shot.


Dublin was more terrified than usual

bombing, three police lorries drove

NEW HAVEN, Conn, Feb. 28.-Two
Yale seniors, Elias w. Harrington and
Ellwood Grissenger, were to-day SEN
fenced for stealing an automobile, Har-
ripgton being given five months in Jail,
while Grissenger was fined 81, 200. They
stole an automobile at Hartford sew
eral months ago, drove it to Bingham
ton, N. Y, where they attended col
lege dance, and then continued to Buff
falo, where Grssenger resides.


They were arrested by Federal agents
under the new Dyer law, and to-day
pleaded guilty before United States
Judge Edwin Thomas. Their counsel
insisted that the affair was college
prank, but District Attorney Smith in
sisted that it was a serious violation
os the Dyer act.


During the war Harrington, who is the

Another demonstration against Presi-
dent Porras took place this afternoon.


Americans are still guarding the
Presidential palace.


Several persons taking part in a dem
onstration before the National Pal
ace shortly before noon were wounded,
one probably mortal]y. United States
soldiers were then sent to guard the
palace, the central squares and stores
where arms and ammunition were
available.


Crowds gathered this morning in the
center Of the city and appointed COM
mittee to wait on President Porras to
demand his resignation because of q
statement made by him Cor publication
to the effect that war between Panama
and Costa Rca over valueless land was
an absurdity.


President Refuses to Resign


President Porras refused to accede
to this, whereupon the committee re-
tired. Later a crowd broke into the
palace through the back entrance.
Guards fired and several of the demon
strators were wounded.


1t has not been learned who called

protection, but soldiers appeared
throughout the city early In the after
noon.

lished the interview with President Por-
ras, has been ordered to suppress ali
mention of political matters.

For todays abrupt upturn in the

1t was simply the sequel to a situa-

signs of improving conditions in out
side trade aZd has been taking its

ther readjuStment remained to be
done with consequent unsettlement
ahead for the snare list.

dence that the real turn for the bet
ter came at the start of the year;

many lines as yet. it is. nevertheless.
positively under way and should in
due time become general.
Those who took the first view have


not only not been buying. but have
been selling stocks short. Those who
took the second view have been quiet
ly accumulating stocks on every

posing positions and it appeared to

for the rise. But it did show that

the control Of those who look for

stocks.

the limit. The veteran had none of

lefts had Lewis hanging on the ropes
when the bell rang.

Los ANGELES, Feb. 16.--Hop Sing

their members, three Of whom we're
killed Tuesday night, when a Chinese
festival was at its height, has famed
to flame 1000 years Of Hop Sing hatred
for the Bing Kong.


In all the coast cities where Chinese
colonies exist the police are taking
every precaution TO prevent further
Tong reprisals. The local Chinatown,
though during the previous night
abustle with activities of celestial
merrymakers rcsembied a silent sep
ulchre tonight The murder of two
Chinese firrchants and the wounding of
a third, B.ng Kong. gunman, has In
jected a profound fear into the life OF
Chinatowns inhabitants. All shops were
closed and doors and windows were bar
ricaded against invasion from an enemy
tong. An unusually large number of
uniformed patroImen appeared in the
streets.


In San Francisco, where one Hop Sing
man was killed and three others were
wounded by rival highbinders. the de-
serted streets Of Chinatown were
strangely silent. while augmented police
squads kept careful watch on the bar
ricaded dens.


The police OF Stockton are investgat
ing the Staying Of Hop Sing man in
that city who was attacked by Bing

A reunion of the Stillman children
took place yesterday in the home of
Mrs. Anne Urquhart Potter Stillman.
at which Miss Anne Stillman, who re-
turned recently from Europe. was the
central figure. 1t was the first time
since the relations of Mr.. and Mrs.
Stillman reached the breaking point
in the spring of 1920 that all the Still
man children were under one roof.
And being Christmas Eve, Miss Still
man naturally played Santa Claus for
her baby brother Guy, whose good
name is questioned in her fathers
divorce suit.


Miss Stillman arrived in New York
Friday on the White Star liner Adri-
attic. She had not sent word she was
coming, and consequently nobody was
at the pier to meet her. She passed
Friday night in the home of friends
on Long Island and motored to her
mothers home, 90 Fifth avenue.
early yesterday. There she found not
only her mother, but her brothers,
James, Jr.. Alexander and baby Guy.
James, or Bud" as he is called, and
Alexander had just arrived home from
school for the holidays. Guy had been
with his mother for several weeks and
was busy figuring out what Santa
Claus should bring him.


After luncheon Miss Stillman went on
shopping trip In her mothers auto
mobile. When she returned home at
s o'clock she was laden with bundles,
the contents Of which we're not disclosed
by Miss Stillman, but which unquestion-
ably contained many articles on Guys
Christmas list.


Many Presents Brought Home.


A reporter for THE NEW York HER
AID met Miss Stillman as she got out
of the automobile. She handed an arm
full of packages to the chauffeur with
Instructions to take them upstairs"
while she proceeded to answer a few
questions.


Eyes I am here with mother for
Christmas" she said. I'VE are all here
that is Bud, Alexander. Guy and my
self?"


Something in the nature of a re-
union" was asked.


Yes"


Has you father been invited?"


Not that I know Of"


did you invite him?''


Il don't think that would be the right
thing to do-do you?"


Alexander stepped out of the elevator
at this junction with the salutation:
Hello, Sis


Where are you going Alexander"
Miss Stillman asked.


For a walk he replied. Want to
come along?"


Miss Stillman replied in the affirma-
tive and turned over to the doorman a
package she was carrying.


Asked IL she had seen her father since
her return Miss Stillman said she had
neither seen nor heard from him. Asked
whether she had broken with Mr.. Still
man she said that sho had not and
admitted that she still entertained hopes
OF effecting a reconciliation between
her father and mother. How this would
be done she would not say.


Dressed In Squirrel Coat.


Miss Stillman wore gray squirrel
coat. brown pleated dress, low cut tan
walking shoes and a black turban hat.
She is somewhat taller than Mrs. STILL
man but of the same general figure
and possesses many OF her mothers
mannerisms.


Although asserting her plans for the
future ARE very indefinite" Miss Still
man said she probably would eat Christ
mas dinner with her mother and BROTH
ers and indicated she might possibly
stay at the Fifth avenue apartment for
the two weeks she Is TO be In New York.
She will return to Paris at the end
of that time and expects to finish school
there in the late spring.


Last Christmas Miss Stilman was
with her father, with whom she had
taken sides when the divorce suit began.
The reconciliation between her and her
mother occurred last autumn before
Miss Stillman sailed for Europe. Just
what caused tho change of mind was
matter Miss Stillman was not in
clined to discuss yesterday. She seemed
to want to forget all about the diff
culties OF her father and mother and
to enjoy Christmas with her brothers,

ing hour, came the crowds went

fight the bandits, who fired three shots,
one Of which, struck Mrs. Mathulek in the
abdomen and seriously wounded her.


The police of East Newark believe that
the bandits intended to hold up the crap
game. but that they entered the wrong
door and got into the barroom instead.
But at the sound of the first shot fired
by the bandits the men in the back room
apparently thought the police had come
for them, and they abandoned their game
and bent their energies toward getting
out. Limousines and touring cars were
parked along the curbing outside the
place, some of the gamblers having come
from Newark and New York. and within
few minutes after the bandits began
shooting the cars were plunging in all
directions at top speed


The gamblers went head first and feet
first through the windows, smashing
every pane of glass in the back room,
and wrecking the chairs and furniture
in their eagerness to reach the open
air None OF these men were hurt, so
far as could be ascertained, and none
OF them saw the bandits. who also
escaped in an automobile.


Mathulek told the police that the six
men came into the saloon and demanded
money, and that he told them he had
no money. The leader of the band said
he would look in the cash register, and
started behind the bar. But Mathulek
started toward him, and the bandit fired
twice, both bullets striking the mirror
behind the bar. Mrs. Mathulek also
started toward him, and the bandit fired
point blank at her when she was no
more than three feet away, the bullet
striking her in the abdomen. The BAN
dts then ran from the saloon without
stealing anything. Mrs. Mathulek was
taken to st. Michaers Hospital in New
ark.
