New York City, Oct. 13-According
to the best information available
here twenty-four persons, including
ten colored members of the American
Southern Syncopated Orchestra per-
ished when the Laird liner, Rowan,
sank off the southwest coast of Scot
land, following two collisions Sun
day


The accident was due to II double
collision in the North Channel off
Corsewall Point early in the morning,
the Rowan first collided with the
West Camak, which she damaged
badly.


Wireless calls brought the Clan
liner Clan Malchom, but the latter in
confusion and heavy fog ran into the
disabled Rowan, which sank immed-
lately.


An official statement says the
Rowan carried ninety-three persons in
Guiding crew and was bound from
Glasgow, Scotland, to Dublin, Ireland.


The West Camak helped in the res
cue work, afterward putting into Glas-
Cow with twenty-siX survivors. Capt.
Donald Brown of Glasgow is reported
to have gone down with the Rowan.
Three other vessels also answered the
call and completed the work of res
cue as far as it was possible.


One of the men known to have died
after being pulled out of the water
was Peter Robinson, drummer.


The Syncopated orchestra which
went to London in June, 1919, gave
performances there and vicinity until
two months ago when they made
tour of Scotland. There were origin
ally 80 members, about 10 of them
British players.

We're thrust into their faces the train

shovel. The noise attracted the atten-
tion OF the engineer. who took his gaze
from the rails a moment to ascertain


shat was wrong.


Stop the train" shouted one of the
masked men. holding pistol toward
the engineer, while another bandit
covered the fireman. The engineer
closed the throttle. but hesitated to ap-
ply the brakes until the robber, stepping
close, poked the barrel OF hts revolver
In the face of the driver and COM
manded GIVE her the air quick"


The engineer stopped the train. The
bandits then commanded the fireman to
uncouple the mail ard the baggage car.
Az soon as these cars were disconnected

TO the cab and ordered the engineer to
proceed.


A mile south of the holdup the rob-
bers commanded the engine crew TO stop.

and fireman guarded In the cab the other
robbers entered the mall car and blew
open the safe. All OF the registered
mail and all of the valuables In the safe
were placed in q bag. The robbers then
carried their plumber TO an automobile.
waved good night to the trainmen and
dashed away in the car.


Released from the commanding muZ-
zles of the bandits pistols. the engineer
and fireman, although they could see
smoke and flames coming from the door
of the mail car quickly backed vp 10
the rest of their train.


The passengers were roaming the
tracks in CONSERVATION trying to ascer-
tain what had happened, as the robbery
had required about an hour. The burn
ing mail car was switched Off the main
track as quickly as possible and the loco
motive and baggage car were connected
to the passenger coaches.


The train then proceeded to Cham
paign twenty miles south. where a new
engine crew picked up the train and pro-
ceeded toward New Orleans.

MEXICO CITY, May 10 (By The Asso-
ciated Press.)--Virtual martial law
prevailed to-day in Morelia, capital Of
Michoacan, the scene Of Thursday
nights fighting between the police and
radicals on one side and Catholics on
the other, in which there were more
than 100 casualties.


Correspondents of Mexico City news
papers in Morelia give varied estimates
of the number of the killed. El Demo
crata says the dead aggregated ten and
the Excelsior fifty, while Ell Universal
says merely that there were 100 vic
Tins.


Federal troops last night displaced
the city police, guarding the streets
and restoring order, and to-day, ac-
cording to dispatches received here,
they were patrolling the streets as a
precautionary measure against further
clashes which were said to be immi-
nent.


Details of last nights occurrences in
dictate that several thousand Catholics,
including many women and children,
marched through the streets, carrying
banners and protesting orally against
the radicals, who were charged with
many sacrilegious outrages.


The police, under Chief Inspector
Vicente Coyt, attempted to dispense
the paraders, and when they refused to
acquiesce the clash followed.


According to the reportss the officers
were Immediately reinforced by radi-
calls among the spectators, many of
whom carried arms. Within few min
utes the streets were filled with fight
ing men, women and children. Shots
We're fired and clubs and fists were
freely used before Federal troops could
be rushed to the scene to quell the
rioting,


The latest dispatches from Morelia to
the Excelsior indicate intense bitter
ness is being manifested against the ex-
IRENE action Of Coyt, which is believed
here to have been unwarranted. Coyt
who led the police personally, was in
jured, and three of his men were among
those killed. Isaac Arriaga, Socialist
leader in Morelia and head of the agra
rian commission there, also was killed

Plumb plan, which the public has un-
equivocally rejected, they can imbue
the national agreement with the same
unpopularity. Doubtless the Plumb
plan leaders are behind the national
agreements. Doubles the continua-
tion of the national agreements will
aid the Plumb plan campaign But the
advocacy of the national agreements
by labor in general can be reasonably
explained without charging labor with
Interior motives. This can be made
clear by tracing the history of these
agreements.


Previous to the war there were no
such contracts as national agreements
in existence. Even in the case of train
service employees, while there had been
arbitration covering large territories
and while there had been national leg
islation in the form of the Adamson
act, prescribing the length of their day,
the agreements or schedules had been
signed by each road with its own en-
ployees, and interpretations and adjust
ments to meet local conditions were
effected by conference between repre-
sentatives of the road and its men.
Oftentimes adjustments or modifica-
tions were made on single division
of railway that did not apply on
other divisions of the same railway.
Nearly all carriers had agreements
with its train service employees. Some
had schedules with other classes. Some
had no other schedules at all. But
there were no national agreements.


With the coming of Federal opera
tion during the war the whole labor
situation was handled on orders from
Washington. The Administration in
sisted that this was necessary as war
measure and that loyal and efficient
service could not otherwise have been
secured. This is probably true, but it
worked in the end to reduce efficiency
and morale on the individual railway,
and the position taken by the Admin
stration does not explain why it was
necessary year after the war was over
to sign national agreement with the
shop crafts and why this practice was
followed with four other organizations,
the last of the five agreements being
signed few days before the roads
vent back into private hands.

Nobody tries nowadays to eat a
quail a day for thirty days. Men
have stopped looking for the North
Pole. But the effort to swim the
English Channel is almost an annual
event. August and early September
are the favored time for it. A couple
of weeks ago the Italian swimmer
TARABosoHI tried and failed; and
there have been one or two other
attempts since.


The mad desire to swim the choppy
sea between Dover and Calais did not
rise in the human breast until 1872.
Three years later the Englishman,
Captain MATTHEW WEBB, succeeded,
making the trip in fifteen minutes
less than twenty-five hours. For three
dozen years after that the Channel
defied all swimmers, but in 1911
THOMAS w. BURGESS accomplished
the crossing in time fifty minutes
slower than WEBB's. The Briton,
who lost his life in the Niagara
Whirlpool. still holds the record.


Swimming the Channel is about
the hardest days work, but unless
Nature takes the Channel away there
will be men and women ambitious to
swim it for a long time. Women
eventually will probably succeed bet
ter than men; they are going at the
water game with spirit not to be
denied.

near here yesterday. TIE victims

daughter. Nerva, seventeen. Another
daughter, Ardith, aged ten years, was

found tonight as to the assailant or
the motive for the crime.

mate, who went to the house today
to visit her chum. Receiving no re-
sponse to her knock, the girl tound
the Monroe house unlocked and enter
ed to discover the tragedy

beaten almost beyond recognition
The bed clothing was undisturbed, in
dicating they were killed while
asleep Against a wall was found
a heavy nail-studded club.


Physicians believe the younger
daughter will recover, although she
was still in a semi-conscious state
tonight.

OSWEGO, N. Y, Jan. l5.--A UNIQUE
municipal tanglc was uncovered this
week when the twelve-year-old dead
lock on the Board of Fire and Police
was the direct cause of bringing state
police here to patrol the CITY, A police
captain and several patrolmen have
been suspended following indictments
IN connection with the disappearance of
two barrels of whisky.


Governor Miller has been asked to
intervene and straighten out the mud
die. In the mean time detail of state
troops is here working with the local
police.


The trouble began about q month ago,
wnen three Scranton men with an auto
truck load Of liquor ran it into a local
garage When they called for it the
following morning the liquor had dis.
appeared. Robert Gougher, owner Of
Captain Charles Edland and Patrolmen

Attorney presented the matter to the
grand jury, with the result that these

missioner Otis, owner Of the garage.

eextortion, grand larceny, impersonat-
ing Federal officers and conspiracy.

pensions depleted the force to the dan
ger point, and the District ATTORNEY.
over the heads of all the other officials,
appealed to the state police and had
troopers sent here.

police force dates back ten or twelve
years. About a decade ago the board
was evenly divided. Two Republicans
and two Democrats For years the city
went along WITHOUT police chief, the
different members of the force acting
in that capacity daily in rotation. Two
years ago the deadlock was broken and
the slate cleaned up. Then another
deadlock came and has remained up to
the present.


The Fire and Police Board met again
Thursday night after the suspensions
and after the state police had entered
the city. Bat the members again re-
fused to break their deadlock and trans
acted only routine business.

called to have another bill for a single
headed commission drafted and sent

PALM BEACH, Fla, Feb. 3.-The
houseboat Victoria, carrying President
elect Harding on his vacation cruise
up the Florida coast. got into difficult
ties again to-day and fell so far behind
her schedule that her distinguished
passengers may leave her tomorrow
or Saturday and complete their trip to
ST. Augustine by rail.


After spending several hours fast in
mud bank in the Indian River, the
Victoria anchored tonight about ten
miles below here. In two days she has
covered only about fifty miles, and
still is $50 miles from st. Augustine,
where Mr.. Harding has an engagement
for Monday. Should further trouble
Develop it is regarded as certain that
the party will make part Of their
return trip overland


The Victoria had several delays dur
ing the day, but her most serious one
occurred short distance above Pom
pano, where she rammed her nose into
the mud and was held so tightly that
her own engines could not extricate
her. She was pulled off by the speed
boat Sea Robin, sent from here by her
owner, j. L. Replogle, the steel man.
The Victoria was not damaged.


The President-elect now is expected
to reach here some time before noon
tomorrow. He will play a game Of
golf, and probably will accept an invi-
tation to dine privately ashore.

II am going to take her to see Santa

fed. permitting the convoy to break

TORRINGTON, Conn, Sept. 6.-Two
persons were killed and two mortally
injured yesterday afternoon when a
seven-passenger touring car hit a
freight train on the Bridgeport- Win


sted branch of the New York, New
Haven & Hartford Railway at Albert
Street crossing.


The automobile. driven by Gureo
Sardie, forty-two years old, of 11e
Roosevelt Street, Torrington, carried
in addition tc members of the Sardie
family, several New York visitors. The
automobile turned a somersault, pin
ming three beneath it. The wreckage
then caught fire and two fire COM
panies were necessary TO save the
bodies from the flames.

| Albert Scarrone, fourteen years old,

Anita Sardie, fourteen years old.


skull fractured and burned. Recovery


doubtful.


| Marble Sardic, sixteen years old, an
| other daughter, was thrown twenty


feet when the car struck. She es-


caped with slight injuries.


| The injured are in Charlotte, Hun


gerford Hospital.


Guireo Sardie owrar of tho r,~ool, - !


automobile, remained unconscious af-
| ter the accident and the only member

Failed to Halt Auto


The freight train had just left Tor
rirgton station, according to the police,
who say it was running less than twenty


miles an hour. When Sardie's automo-
bile struck the train five cars had gone


over the crossing. The cause of the &C


cident was given as Sardie's inability to
the freight trains approach. He is said
by eyewitnesses of the accident to have
had trouble with the brakes
The radiator of the automobile ran


under freight car and was twisted
off. the torn metal becoming entangled
on rods Of the cars underbody. 1t was
dragged fifty feet and then turned over.
The two dead children were visible
beneath the wreckage of the overturned


car. which caught fire. Two fire COM
panies responded to an alarm and a
squad of police from the Torrington
station arrived within five minutes of
the wreck. Efforts of bystanders to


remove the bodies proved futile be-


cause of the flames. Firemen extri-

can't be far from land if there are birds

you had the meal you wished for"

JACKSONVILLE, Fla, Jan. 30.-The
italian steamer Nettuno, bound from
Port Arthur, Tex, TO Brindisi, Italy
was towed into this port to-day by. the
coast guard cutter Yamacraw, after
being afire at sea.


Captain Bersini, on arriving here,
attributed the saving of his ship to
mlracle-the explosion of her fuel oil
tanks, which literally snuffed out the
fire after it had ragged unchecked for
twenty hours. The blaze originated in
the engine room from bursting feed
pipe when the Nettuno was feur days
cut from Port Arthur, from which she
cleared on January 21 with a cargo of
gasoline and fuel oil. At that time
she was off the Florida coast in the
vicinity of Bermuda


In few moments the Nettuno was
seething inferno amidships and it
did not seem possible for her to re-
main afioat but short time, Captain
Bersini stated.


Describes 20 Hours of Horror


Seated in his badly damaged cabin
while the Nettuno swung easily at
anchor in the river, Captain Bersini
described vividly the horror through
which the ships personnel lived while
the fire ragged unchecked and the ship
wallowed helplessly in heavy seas. The
crew fought with desperation to keep
the fires from the gasoline stored in
the hold. The fight, however, appeared
hopeless, according to Captain Bersini,
and momentarily he expected the flames
to reach the gasoline and blow the
ship to atoms.


Virtually every lifeboat the Nettuno
carried either had been carried away
or smashed by the terrible buffeting
the tanker sustained during the hours
the fire twisted and wrecked her en-
gine room and warhead and cracked
her steel decks and sideplates. The
fact that the crew had no .lifeboats in
which to leave the burning vessel
added to the seriousness of the situa-
ton.


Engineer Shows Heroism


Captain Bersini praised the work of
the chief engineers, Betteno and Crosa,
as we'll as of Engineer Landi Joanna,
Who volunteered to 60 below at the
time the feed pipe burst to shut off
the flow of oil and rescue two firemen
trapped in the freroom. Joanna was
so severely burned that Captain Ber-
could survive. His clothing was
burned from his body and his flesh in
many places literally cooked.


Joanna and the two firemen, Branca-
laone and Losito, who also were severe
ly burned, were transferred to the Bel
gian steamship Kremlin on January 26,
the day after the fire aboard the Net
tuno had been extinguished, and sent
to Newport News.


The Y.macraw, which had been ad-
vised to look out for the Nettuno,
picked up the ship on January % and
headed for Jacksonville.

is estimated that it will be weeks be-
fore she 10 auo;r roadu for caa

New Jerseys new state constabu-
larry will this week begin actual serv-
ice. There has been a struggle for
years to secure such force, but at
last law creating it. was enacted,
and for three months the men have
been in camp under training for
their work.


No state needs such service more
than New Jersey. Lying between
the first and third cities of America
and with its coast lined with pleas
ure resorts, it's suburban regions
have long been infested by maraud-
ers and highwaymen from the cities,
while its highways are frequented to
an exceptional degree by both pleas
ure and business vehicles. 1nnumer-
able motor trucks nightly traverse
the highway between New York and
Philadelphia, passing for !. miles
through woodland and sparsely set
tied farmlands, while uncounted pas
senger cars constantly go through
little populated regions.


The new force, while it will help,
will scarcely meet the need. New
Jersey is not large state, but it is
far too large for company of sew
enty-nine men to be able to patrol
even its most important roads, to say
nothing of other duties which they
may at times be called upon to
perform.

To THE NEW York HERALD: For q
number of years the ailanthus trees in
the yards back of me In West Tenth
street have been way stations for

Spring and fall they afford me the pleas
ure Of welcoming some old friends. Of
bidding godspeed to them on their long

bers and variety.

Off with the coming Of dusk; and one

More than 100000 separate freight
rate readjustments have been effected
since the Interstate Commerce Commits
sion authorized the last blanket increase
in transportation rates last summer, ac-
cording to survey made by the Asso-
citation Of Railway Executives. In
nearly all cases these revisions have
been downward in recognition of rate
inequalities resulting from a series Of
successive increases over period of
years and causing restricted movement
In certain commodities and localities


Although railway executives adhere
to the belief that no general reduction of
freight tariffs can be effected until lower
operating expenses and increased ton
mage restore the earning power Of the
carriers, the records show that the
process of ironing out disproportionate
bumps" In the rate structure has been
going forward steadily since the sum-
mer of 1920.


The Transcontinental Freight Bureau
of Chicago reports that 153.319 reduc-
tons have been made in eastbound
domestic rates. 1872 in westbound tar
ifs. and 120 In export and import rates
affecting grain. iron, steel, food prod
ucts, lumber and many other commodi-
ties and covering generally shipments
from or to California, Oregon, Wash
ington. Montana, Utah. Idaho, Wyoming
Nevada, Arizona and New Mexico to
or from points east of the Rocky Noun
tains to the Atlantic seaboard.


In the last year the Western Trunk
Line Committee has brought about over
1000 downward establishments in the
tariffs on crushed rock, gravel, building
materials. grain, coal, lumber, live stock
foods. molasses, hides. fruits, vegetables.
and other commodities. The reductions
ranged from 5 per cent. to 70 per cent,
the maximum cut being applied to paper
and lumber.


The Trunk Line Association of New
York has acted upon 2.463 rate revision
proposals out Of a total of 2,662 taken
up since September l last; while $50
and 159 downward readjustments have
been made respectively by the New
England Freight Association and the
Southwestern Freight Bureau.

NOME, Alaska, Jan. 19.xThomas
Ward, president and general manager
Of the Ward Copper Company, of New
York, was found frozen to death about
twenty miles from Teller, Alaska, Jan
uary II, according to word reaching
Nome to-day.

camp, in the inner Seward peninsula,
with an Esquimau man and woman
and two dog teams, en- route to Teller,
reindeer station on Grantly Harbor.
After reaching the top Of the divide
above Teller the three became lost in
the darkness. The Esquimaus said they
decided to go back to cabin they had
seen, but Ward proceeded on alone.


For the next two days, the Esqui-
maus said, they we're stormbound in
the cabin, and on the third day battled
their way into the station, only to
learn that Ward had not arrived. A
searching party started out the next
day, and found Wards sled and dog
team on Dewey Creek. There were evil
dences that Ward had spent the night
there. The temperature during the
night had been 20 degrees below zero.
and Ward was known 20 have only a
robe to protect him from the cold

Ward evidently had left his team on
the morning of the 18th and started for
Teller, ten miles distant. He probably
became confused, they said, and headed
in the Wronu direction

LONDON, March 14-Six young
lrishmen convicted of killing members
of the Grown forces in Ireland were
hanged in Mountioy prison, Dublin.
this morning, while twenty thousand
people knelt in prayer in the streets
about the prison and all business and
public activity in the city was sus-
pended.


The prisoners were hanged in mfrs.
at 6, Z and o'clock Two of them,
Patrick Moran and Thomas Wheelan.
We're convicted by a courts martial for
taking part in the Dublin shootings of
Bloody Sunday, Novembe 21 last. The
others, Thomas Bryan, Patrick Dovle.
Bernard Ryan and Francis Flood. were
found guilty Of high treason in the at
tempted ambush of police at Drum
conds' near Dublin, in January. Flood,
the youngest, was nineteen years old.
and none of the others was more than
twenty eight years old.


Thousands Join in Prayers


Extraordinary efforts had been made
to obtain communication of the sem
tences, and appeals were sent to the
Premier and King. Last night how
ever, 1T became apparent that the exc
cutlons would be carried out, and
tnousands of persons quietly assem-
bled outside the prison walls and re-
clted the prayers for the dying until
the curfew forced them indoors.


As soon as the ban was lifted This
morning the thousands began reas-
sembling. Holy statues and pictures
were placed on the prison walls and
on the streets and hundreds in the
death watch carried lighted candles.
The occasional weeping of some woman
or the raised voice of priest reciting
prayers was the only sound that rose
above the murmur of the thousands
recltlng prayers, except the occasional
clank and rattle of armored cars as
they patrolled the streets. Just before
the time of the executions, however.
the arnored cars were withdrawn from
the streets.


The wife Of Patrick Doyle was among
those who kept the death vigil in the
street. One of their three children
died two days ago and the funeral was
set for to-day. Mrs Doyle collapsed,
however, before the last of the execu-
tions and was taken to a hospital.


Mother Proud of Doyle


Doylcs mother was another of the
watchers, but she remained calm and
prayerful throughout the ordeal. After
it was all over she said: ~ am proud
to have reared so good boy and
prouder still that | reared him to die
for Ireland"


The civil authorities were not invited
to witness the executions and no de-
tails were given out, but it is known
that mass was celebrated in the mems
cells before the execution. 1t is said
that the eXecutioner was taken into the
prison inside tank last Saturday.


At 1920 O'Clock an official bulletin
was posted outside the prison walls,
announcing that the executions had
taken place The crowds then dis
persed, many OF the persons going to
masses in the various churches while
hundreds attended the funeral services
for the Doyle child.


Shops and Offices Closed
From early morning until noon shops
and Offices were closed, the street cars
did not operate and even the postal,
telephone and telegraph services were
discontinued.


Alexander Carlisle WHO recently tele-
eraphed Arthur Griffith, Vlce-President
Of Sim Fein. for authority to reopen
peace negotiations, was referred by
Griffith to the Dali Eireann After to-
days hangings he wired to the Dali
Eireann: II trust the British people
soon will realize it's mismanagementi in
ireland and leave the government of
Ireland to the Irish, letting the Welsh
men, Canadians and others look after
their own affairs. Can you authorize
my Saturdays proposals?' %

. LONDON. Dec. 13.-Absence of de-
tails over the increasing unrest in
India led to the belief today that the
British have established a censorship
on all dispatches from that country.


There is much anxiety over the
Indian situation. The apprehension
was heightened by news that the
natives in Allahabad boycotted the
visit of the Prince of Wales. The
streets through which the prince
drove were absolutely empty.

throughout India of both men and
women. Gandi. leader of the non-
co-operationists, ordered only passive
resistance, but despite this measure
disorders have occurred.


Mandalay and Rangoon. in Burma,

CAIRO. Egypt. December 24.-Dis-
orders in connection with the Egypt
ian nationalist agitation broke out
today in Gizeh. a suburb of Cairo
when a party of students raided the
government survey offices. British
troops were rushed from Cairo to
cope with the disturbance. The stu
dents were ultimately elected. The
native losses were given in the early
reports as five killed and twenty
wounded.


While the disorders were proceed
ing in Gizeh. Cairo itself remained
quiet, and no disturbances from the
provinces were reported with the ex-
ception of MINOR troubles at Tanta
fifty miles northwest of Cairo.


The authorities conveyed to Suez
today six followers of Said Zagloul
Pasha, the nationalist leader fortibly
removed from the city yesterday,
whom Field Marshal Allenby, the
British high commissioner in Egypt
had ordered expelled from Cairo.


Cairo bristled with police and
cled over the delta of the Nile. fol-
lowing disturbances.


Said Zagloul Pasha's removal came
as a result of his refusal to obey an
order issued by the military authori-
ties that he and his chief followers
cease all political activity and leave
Cairo.


Although much wanton destruction
occurred during the disturbances. the
authorities claim that the situation
need not be regarded with particular
anxiety. The disturbances appear to
have been confined to Cairo.

Texas-Mississippi circuit will start on
January Is and end February 10, with
San Antonio, Dallas, Houston, Fort
Worth and New Orleans being the CEN

time to reach Florida for the tourna-
ments, which start at Jacksonville.

an outlaw, the other a deputy sheriff.
stood In the streets of this mountain
town this afternoon and pumped bullets
into each others bodies until one died
and the other was badly injured. The
dead man is Kelly Robinson, a thirty
year-old mountaineer, who had been
known for a long time as a desperate.
The wounded man Is Deputy Sheriff
John Smith. youth of % years.


Robinson was paroled few days ago
from the Kentucky reformatory. where
he had been sent to serve term for
murder. He came to Hazard to-day and
terrorized the town before being run
out. He returned later and shot at
Smith. when the latter accosted him. His
first shot missed. Smith got his artil-
lery into action without delay. and as
the heavy pistols roared people ran
from every direction to see the duel
Smith was shot twice. and though badly
wounded kept his gun turned on Rob-
inson. He shot the outlaw twice with
out visible effect. but when the third
bullet struck him. Robinson's legs
crumpled and he fell dead. Smith fell

Faculty athletic advisers of the
high schools are wrestling with their
annual problem. that of procuring a
court for the scholastic league basket
ball games With the opening of the
championship series less than a month
distant. no satisfactory playing floor
has been found. and it now seems that
the schools must pay out a consider
able sum of money for hall in which
to conduct the engagements. For
several weeks. the advisory board
has been casting about for a playing
floor. but in all instances where pro-
prietors of establishments have been
approached the high school folk have
been politely rebuffed.


The only gymnasium owned by the
schools that really is large enough
for the game is at Central High
School. but the galleries are not of
SUFFICIENT size to accommodate the
throngs that attend the contests
1t appears that the schools will have
to return to the Coliseum, where the
series was played last winter. While
ideally located. this hall lacks room
for spectators and the heavy rental
demanded would severely tax the ath-
letic associations exchequer.


An effort was made to obtain the
Arcade for the series. but faculty ad-
visers were informed that under no
consideration could that spacious floor
be used for basket ball. Catholic
University gymnasium, used by the
high schools hseveral seasons ago. and
the Congress Heights auditorium, well
equipped for the basket game. were
considered. but the board decided
these halls were too far from the
heart of the city for the convenience
of the pupils.

Yom Kippur. the most solemn festl-
val in the Jewish calendar, will begin
at sunset tomorrow and end at sun
set Wednesday. During the twenty
four hours worshipers will abstain
from food and drink and, divorclng
themselves from the outer world, de-
vote the day to meditation and prayer
In the orthodox synagogueS there is
no cessation from worship during the
fasting period. Many of the most de-
yout Jews do not leave the house OF
worship from the time they enter on
Tuesday until nightfall Wednesday.


Yom Kippur is the day of atone
ment for sins committed during the
wear and marks the closing Of the
neuitential season. which begins with
New Year day, ten days previous
Probably the most impressive services
during the day is that memorable
ing the dead. Prayers are offered for
the repose of the souls of those dear
ones who have gone before. and the
music, specially arranged for the oc-
casion, is in keeping with the serv-
ices.


The day devoted to penitence and
PRAYER closes when the shofar, or
rams horn, is sounded, dismissing the
congregation. Local Jewish congre-
cations plan to observe the day with
great solemnity.

beside the bed and died instantly

hurried to the Barnett Hospital in
Paterson, where it was said their

shot through the head. The photog-

MILAN, Italy, April 26.-The Social
lists IN Fiume grew panic stricken when
they thought the election was going
against them. Mayor Zanella and the
town councillors bolted unanimously.
rallied a large body of Croatians and
Communists to their standard and re-
tanned control of the city


Disorders broke out and twelve per-
sons were wounded when the Croats
and Socialists exchanged shots. A
body of carabineers restored quiet.


Toll keepers at the elections to-day
expressed the opinion that the Social
lists actually had won the elections by
a few hundred majority. Not knowing
this, however, and becoming frantic
with their fears of defeat, the Social
lists burned the ballot boxes. A new
election is now being planned.


FIUME, April 25 (By The Associated
Press Count Caccia- -Dominioni, the
Italian Minister, left Fiume to-day
aboard a torpedo boat destroyer owing
to the rioting. The frontier has been
closed by a brigade of infantry.

were badly burned.

MEXICO CITY, Aug. l6.-The Aguila,
Corona and Royal Dutch petroleum
companies and the Shell Transport and
Trading Company to-day announce
their intention to suspend operations
in the oil fields. These companies are
the only large producers still operat-
ing, the American companies having
suspended some time ago. They had
been able 70 continue because Of the
preferential terms Of their charters
which exempt them from paying pro-
duction taxes.


General Obregon, however, recently
changed this tax to a stamp tax, from
which the companies are not exempt
ed, thus placing them on the same
footing with American producers and
forcing them also 70 shut down.

LONDON, April 2.-According to
London news report from Berlin the
Krupp factories at Essen have now
1000 more employees than before the
war. The Krupp interests now employ
in all $1,000 persons, of whom $4,000
are in the Essen works and the re-
mander at the Germania shipyards and
in minor undertakings.

and casting operations of the Essen
plant the factory is now producing
seventy-tive kinds of machines. appa-
ratus and technical articles. From a
new rust-proof steel, which does not
corrode even in boiling nitric acid, are
being made many articles, including
palates and teeth, which replace gold.
The construction of railway material
and rolling stock also has attained
enormous dimensions, according to the
report.

ant strain when on the pike they

breaking-up confesses. And you

hear the creaking of your bones

and you could lay the fighters

You hobble DER the paving
stones, your face is most forbid
ding; your knees are spawned,
CATER Jones, your feet are al

old friends present, for that's

With the speculative community ap-
parently even more satisfied that, the


railroad situation would be untangled
| in manner not unfavorable to stock
holders, the stock market, freed from
the restraints caused by the railroad
crisis, yesterday continued the up
ward movement which started Tues
day. Trading was light and originated
largely among professional spectators.
The railroad shares, which were
again distinctly firm, went further in
the process of wiping out the losses in
Cured last week before the strike
order was made public, while specu-
iators in advance sensed trouble.
Leadership, however, was seized by the
shares of domestic oil concerns. espe-
cially Pacific Oil, which for weeks have
been rising at the marketplace, while
the quotations of crude oil have been
ascending. The speculation for fur
ther increase in the quotation of oil
shares is based on the assumption
that the decentralization in the industry
is over. Obviously, the upset equilb-
rum between supply and demand ear
lier In the year was temporary re-
flection of upset business conditions
rather than a symptom of a oerma-
nently unhealthy condition of the oil
trade. During the earlier critical
period the reaction in oil shares of
solid companies clearly went too far


An attempt on the part of traders to
stop the upturn yesterday by selling
Mexican Petroleum was fruitless.


The chief exception to the general
market trend was again the steel group,
which was heavy yesterday because
what spectators suspected in the pre-
vious day was verified by the event.
Republic Steel and Iron earnings for the
third quarter, which were to a large
extent only of historical interest, since
lately the curve has started moderately
upward, were the most unsatisfactory
thus far during this year of extreme
depression in the steel industry. The
United States Steel Corporation and
Midvale will make public their quar-
terly statements next week


In sympathy with another marked
rise in the dollar value of the pound
sterling, European exchanges were
firmer yesterday. Cotton quotations
closed slightly higher and, after ex-
treme fluctuations, wheat prices at the
final sales were moderately above those
Of the previous day.

When Thomas Mcdonald, T. of 60C
Grove street. Jersey City. fell into
fifteen feet of water off the old Dream
land pier, Coney Island, yesterday
afternoon, two rescuers sprang into
action. One was Cecilia Stackhouse
IA, schoolgirl, of 1915 Seventieth
street. Bay Ridge, and the other a
woman who was with her, Mrs. Mae
Genovese Of the same address. Mrs
Genovese could swim only a few
strokes and the girl couldn't swim at
ALL


Cecilia jumped into the water. The
boy could be seen struggling dozen
feet from the pier, and making a
strong effort; the girl landed within a
few feet of him. The throng, watch
ing what was regarded as the every
day act Of one kid pulling another out
of danger. saw the girl sink and then
appear with a look of terror on her
face.


II can't SWIM" she shouted before
she went down a second time


Mrs. Genovese. who had run along the
pier to a point opposite the girl and the
boy, forced her way through the crowd,
and. without even removing her hat.
sprang into the water. She followed
young Mcdonald and the girl to the
bottom, but when she came UP again the
two children were near her and she had
the presence Of mind to seize them and
shove them toward the piling OF the pier.
Then she managed to force herself
within reaching distance of the piles.
She wrapped enc arm around one of
them, reached out and drew the boy and
the girl to her and held them afioat until
help could reach her.


Robert Ober and William Hoffman,
life guards. who had been called. reached
the woman just as she was beginning to
tire. They took the children from her
and lifted them to persons on the pier.
They then swan to the beach with Mrs.
Genovese.


The boy was unconscious when taken
from the water. For almost an hour tn Q
life guards worked over him. assisting
DIR. Duboise OF Coney Island Hospital.
Then he opened his eyes and recognized
his mother, Mrs. Bedelia Mcdonald, who
was being attended for fainting spells on
n str etcher beside him. He was taken
to Coney Island Hospital. where II was
said he would be discharged to-day.


Persons who witnessed Mrs. Genovese s
rescue of the children said they would
recommend her as a candidate for a
Carnegie hero medal Members of the
United States Live Saving Service said
they would indorse the recommendation.

least fourteen known dead, thirty in
jured and property damage that will
amount to hundreds of thousands of
dollars resulted from two wind and
rain storms which swept widely separ-
ated parts of Arkansas last night and
early this morning.


At Malvern the tornado knocked down
homes and outhouses as it swept path
200 feet wide clear of all timber and
other obstacles. One farmer was killed
and his three children were seriously
injured at one place. and two persons
met death at another.


A family of eight persons was killed
near Mena, in the western part of the
state, when their home was demolished.
Near Arkadelphia one person was
killed and twenty -four were injured
when the tornado brushed lumber
camp.

cameramen who found the three digni-
taries at the Pennsylvania Station

| separate private cars, each surrounded
by his own staff

ing Of these three great national fig
ures would have involved some diplo-
matte dickering and the unwinding of
red tape, but the photographers used
the direct method. Admiral Beatty,
when told what the men wanted, merely
grinned and stepped out to be
"mugged," but an aide of the Italian
general insisted his chief could not
engage in so undigniHed proceeding.

approached through the usual formal
channels.

the conversation was about he brushed
the fussy aide aside and stalked up to
Admiral Beatty, who shook hands with
him. The Belgian general hastened to
join the group. "Click!" went ten
cameras and the job was done.

W1LKES-BARRE, Pa, Jan. 16.-The
store and home Of James A. Joyce.
Pittston merchant and leader of the
Pennsylvania Coal Company miners,
was wrecked and several other houses
were badly damaged at 4:30 o'clock
this morning by an explosion of dyna-
mite. Four men have been arrested
by the Pittston police, who believe
miners of the Pennsylvania Coal Com
pany, who are displeased with the
stand that Joyce has taken in the
present strike situation, are respon-
sible for the blast. Joyce led the
miners to victory in the fall and the
coal cutters are now getting more
money than ever before. His recent
policy has been to restrain the men
from striking because he believed they
did not have just cause.


He pitted his eloquence against the
insistence of radical insurgents at a
meeting of the general grievance com
mlttee last night, and although he
d!d not win his point definitely, neither
did the other side win. and when the
meeting adjourned conditions were
badly muddlcd.


Police Prohibit Miners Meeting


John L. Lewis, international presi-
dent Of the United Mine Workers, was
here to-day. 1t was intended that ne
should meet with the Pittston miners,
but the Pittston police issued orders
against meeting of any kind within
the city limits.


Some miners favor striking to-mor-
row. and others favor remaining at
work. The former are called insur-
gent radicals, and the latter are most
ly English speaking miners. A meet
ing was to have been held tomorrow
night, at which time the representa-
tives of the 10000 miners would get
report of the meeting of their COM
mittee with President Lewis this after
noon. Since all meetings have been
declared off, it is considered likely
that work will be resumed. Lewis has
declared against a strike. Hc left here
tonight.


Joyce's store is on North Main
Street, Pittston. Last week his life
was threatened many times, but he
showed no fear


Ten houses have been dynamited
here in the last four months, nearly
all owned by. Italians, but this is the
first time that a resident of Joyce's
prominence was placed in danger.


Three persons were sleepin.- in the
house and were thrown from their beds
to the floor. The entire front of the
store was blown out and the stairs
leading to the bedrooms wrecked.
Panes of glass were broken throughout
the house and large section of the
stone foundation caved in. The North
End Garage was badly damaged and
windows in the Pittston Laundry and
Greek Catholic Church were broken.


Appeal for Police Protection


Four arrests Of men previously sus-
pected of dynamiting have been made
and patrol has been placed at the
Joyce home. Mine %, emcn and others
who have counseled ,gainst the strike
fear for their lives and have made ap-
peals for police protection.


Besides the Pittsron police the entire
troop of state police, located at Wy
oming, are searching for the men who
committed the crime. The valleys
prominent residents are making. insist
ent demands that some of the large
force of Secret Service ren now oper-
ating here against he brewers turn
their attention to the strike conditions
and get the leaders.


The whole trouble has beer caused
because the 100 or more men of No. IA
Local, United Mine Workers, refuse to
grant the insurgents q union charter

DUBLIN, Jan. 16.-The whole section
of north Dublin was cordoned by SOL
diers and police last evening and to-
day. The street railway service along
the north quay was suspended. The
center Of the cordoned district includes
Church Street and the place where the
military were ambushed recently and
North King Street, the scene of fierce
fighting in the Easter rebellion.


Houses commanding tha streets in the
occupied district were entered and the
inhabitants of the upper floors given
twenty minutes in which to move down
stairs.


Machine guns were placed in windows
and barbed wire entanglements erected.


The entire area was enclosed, and the
inhabitants are virtually prisoners.
Searchlights tonight are making the
streets as bright as day.


A total area of square mile is sur
rounded, and the biggest raid Dublin
has yet experienced has been under way.
Only the military have been engaged
inside the Gordon, and it is believed
every house will be systematically
searched, the raid lasting several days.
Hundreds of soldiers are taking part,
and field kitchens are providing them
with food.


CORK, Jan. 16.--Serious disorders
followed the shooting here yesterday
in which two detectives in plain clothes
were wounded. The disorders occurred
while a crowd was dispensing from a
football match and parties of police
were trying to clear the streets. Alto
gether twelve persons were wounded
during promiscuous firing, while Excise
Officer Pring was killed by stray shot
from a passing lorry.


The excise officer had come to his
home here for the weekend and was
walking in the street with his brother
and sister.


BELFAST, Jan. 16-Crown forces on
Saturday swept through with great
thoroughness South Armagh, the scene
recently of alleged Sim Fein activities.
Troops and constabulary of the Ulster
Specials" cooperated. Every road was
under supervision. More than 800
prisoners were taken in the various
nets, but after rigorous examination
only forty persons were held in the
military barracks.

Trees are beautiful, but they lack a
certain kind of useful intelligence.
They have a wonderfully developed
sense of form and color and a strong
desire to serve men and birds, and
they also give refuge to insects
whose interests seem to be contrary
to the interests Of men. 1t is against
the fruit trees that a critic would
lodge his loudest complaint. These
trees are famous for their beauty and
their sweetness, but they seem to lack
good sense. Their chief fault is that
they are credulous-too trusting.
Though repeatedly deceived by dour
February. wicked March and some
times by tlighty little April, year after
year they expose the treasure Of their
bloom to the first fair and smiling
days that come. And then the smiling
month turns a cold shoulder on them
and sets the cruel frost upon them.
Now, after hot, dry and uncomforta-
BILE summer, they begin preparations
for a winter rest, though really dur
ing last summer fruit trees did but
little more useful work than most peo-
pie. Then comes a bright day in Octo
ber-a few bright days-and the fruit
trees. ever gulIible and foolish, put
out flowers. And this in October. with
November and December on their way
down from the north! In many Wash
ington gardens you may see fruit
trees in bloom.

along the Sakaria River, at point
about half way between Eski-Shchr
and Mustapha Kemal's capital.
Since then there has been heavy
fighting without any progress. The
Greek army has now recrossed the
Sakaria and is retiring toward
Eski-Shehr. AS was the case when
the Greek offensive toward Eski-
Shehr and Afum-Karahissar col
lapsed last spring, the Turkish
troops have been either too cx-
hausted or too poorly organized to
make an effective pursuit.


Constantine's second reverse
leaves more Turkish territory in
his hands than he held after the
April retirement. But his strate-
gic position is not improved. He
has not conquered the Turks. His
armies are much further from their
sea bases than they were before
and have long lines of communica-
tion to maintain. They have also
suffered heavy losses. The favor
able season for military operations
III the rough Anatolian mountain
region is nearly over. To keep a
reinforced army on new front and
to garrison the broad area behind
it will probably overstrain Greece's
present resources.


The Anatolian war has been tne
without reason. The Kemal gov
ernment repudiated the obligations
which Turkey assumed when her
ENJOYS begged the Allies for an
armistice. 1t defed the Entente
powers and entered into an alliance
with Moscow. 1t was spelling for
fight and eager to eject Greece
from the Asian territory assigned
her by the Sevres Treaty. Now
Kemal has all he can do to hold
on to Angora.


Greece, on the other hand, could
have remained in possession of her
Asia Minor holdings had she been
contented to play the role assigned
her by the peace treaty. She pre-
ferred, however, to change her role
and to estrange the Allies by re-
calling Constantine. His restoration
compelled her to fight for what she
could have had without fighting.
The score in that foolish adventure
isn't yet paid in full. Constantine's
colossal vanity and selfshness and
the folly of the invitation to him
to come back saddled on Greece
cruel and needless sacrifices, of

text:
When China proposed in the Wash
ington conference that all the treaties
among nations affecting her and her
vital interests be made public for the
determination of their scope and va
lidity. she did, by long odds. the big
gest thing that has been done by any
nation at the conference. For gen.
erations the white powers have been
meeting in secret and entering into
treaties relating to China without con-
sulting her. Among the powers that
have thus indulged the most have
been England and France. 1t is said
in Washington that this proposal has
created far more CONSERVATION among
the white nations than any other of
China's proposals has caused in yell
low circles. Unhappily, China has not
always been represented in Office by
honest men. More than once has she
been sold by these-which means that
more than once have nations pretend
ing to a higher civilization than
China bribed Chinese officials into the
betrayal of their country. While the
complete cleansing of the Chinese sit
uation seems beyond the possibility
of the conference, the more light that
is let in and the more wrongs that are
righted the better will it be for all
the world through the years to come.

The Kings colors were carried to VIC

persons lost money on the race, they
saw the race of a lifetime.


Dick Marsh. the Kings trainer, chose
the right sized prize and the right sized
field for the prize. the field being a
small one, only one other horse COM
peting. This was Winter King, whose
jockey, Steve Donoghue. probably is the
greatest Jockey on the English turf since
Fred Archer.


The distance run was mile and
half. The going was hard, but the
weather was fine. The horses got off
with good start, but crawled in pro-
cessional fashion around the field to the
amazement of the spectators, who al
ways expect to see a. rafting pace when
Donoghue rides. His mount this time,
however, was giving the royal horse
nineteen pounds and, therefore, Dono-
ghue permitted him to make the pace.

Jockeys espied the finishing post and IN
creased their speed to such an extent
that the winner actually was galloping
when he passed the judges box in the
wonderful time of three minutes and
three seconds. The jockeys looked more
tired than the horses when the race was
over.


The betting was eleven to four on
Winter King and was about the same
on Bowood never winning again. The
crowd felt that 1t was pity the King
was not present TO see his horse when
the racer was up to the trainers expec-
tations and at the same time TO witness
his first victory this season.


1t was the first match that Donoghue

cloth with which the leader of the gang

countryside near where the outlaws van
ished. but the pursuers have not found

President HARDING is a business
man as well as a statesman. Secre-
tary of the Treasury MELLON, Budget
Director DAWES, Secretary OF War
WEEKS and other heads of depart
ments and bureaus under the Har-
ding Administration are business
men. And these business men who
are the driving power in the admin
istrative branch of the United States
Government knew the day they went
into Office that they had to swing the
broadaxe ON the national expendi-
lures for the reason that the public
could not stand the taxes and the
Treasury could not pay the nations
bills.


In the fiscal year ending with June
80 the tax collections fell more than
$500, 100000 below those Of the year
before. This was not because the
tax rates had been reduced; it was
because business profits. American
incomes and individual incomes, on
which were laid the taxes, had gone
down.


In the same way the tax collections
will be still lower for the present
fiscal year ending with next June.
But the business administration Of
the United States Government has
also anticipated this fall in revenues.
1t has chopped away unflaggingly at
the national expenditures-chopped,
in many instances, far below the
amounts actually appropriated by
Congress. So, thanks to them, the
national Treasury has not become
empty and will not.

5 the Budget Director will present to
Congress his estimate for the next
fsral year ending June so, 1928. 1t
will be down to three billions Of dol
lars in round numbers, or more than
a billion of dollars below the prelim-
mary estimates and half billion of
dollars below the final figures for the
present fiscal year.


The business capacity and financial
sense Of the Harding Administration,
while relieving the public which
foots the bills, has been keeping the
Treasury solvent, though the old
sources of revenue, to which an in
competent or Indifferent Congress
has clung, have been drying up.

CHICAGO, July 7.-Chicago and much
of the middle west today we're still in
the grip of a record breaking heat wave,
with the local weather bureau announc-
ing no relief in sight. The thermometer
here. which registered 50 early this
morning. was steadily rising, after a
sweltering night, when thousands sought
the beaches and parks. which had been
opened for sleeping purposes.


The heat yesterday was held directly
responsible for five deaths and dozens
of prostrations in Chicago. while health
officars asserted the city's mortality
rate had been doubled. One large foun-
dry concern laid off 5000 men because
the heat was too great to continue
work.


Des Moines. Iowa. reported there had
been no break in super-normal tempera-
lures in thirty days, with the maxi
mum daily reading there averaging a
fraction above 81 degrees. Farmers in
Iowa reported corn had been growing
one inch every twenty-four hours for
the last two weeks

SAMARA, Russia, Sept. (By The
Associated Press) Hunger and death
so virtually unnotced in the neglected
streets and alleys of Snmara. Refu-
gees from famine districts near this
city, estimated from thirty to fifty
thousand, are huddled together in de-
serted buildings. unused factories
tattered tents and in wagons massed
about the open spaces about the rail
way stations and docks along the volga
River.


Hunger, typhus, cholera and exhaus-
tion are carrying off hundreds of these
miserable fugitives. young children
falling victims readily to the famine
and its attendant scourges. Bedraggled
and ragged refugees are constantly car
rying pine collins toward the cemetery
where Imprinted wooden crosses mark
hundreds of new graves which have
been dug since the fight before the ad-
vancfng famine began. From SO to
100 starving children are gathered up
daily from the streets or turned over
to the central refuge by parents who
cannot feed them. Many of these little
sufferers have typhus fever but the
hospitals are without beds and mcdi-
cine.


Told Food Is on Way


Samara's only newspaper, single
sheet of brown paper, has printed an
announcement that the American Re-
lief Administrations workers have
reached Moscow and that 800 900 tons
ct American food are en- route to Rus
STA. The discouraged and hungry pop
ulation, however, is loath to believe
that aid will come, and, with Russian
stoicism, the thousands of refugees
moving through this great railway cen
ter arc camping along the highways
and endeavoring to obtain railway rides
to any place where food may be secured


Vladimir Soksolsky, chairman of the
Samara Provincial Soviet, said last
week that 500 carloads of seed grain
have already arrived from Moscow and
that enough was expected to enable
the peasants of Samara Province to
SOW approximately 100000 acres of
wheat for the next harvest. Samara
usually plants an area of ten times
this extent, but this year the area
sown amounted to only 100000 acres
and the crop was almost a failure be-
cause of the drought.

Berlin with ten operetta theatres has
now deprived Vienna of her fame as
the operetta centre Of the world. Franz
Lehar and other Vienna composers who
preferred to give their premieres in
the Austrian capital and capture for
eign markets by pleasant transactions
over Vienna coffee tables now almost
invariably come to Berlin with their
new works.


This practice which has gradually de-
veloped during the past year will be a
confirmed habit during the coming
season. Lehar will have not less than
four premieres in Berlin. "Frasquito"
and THE Yellow Jacket" will be pre-
sented at the Metropole Theatre. to-
gether with a musical version of Ber-
nard Shaw's ''Pygmalion," while one
act piece entitled Spring will be
heard on rival stage.


The chief complaint about the Ger
man productions Is their lack 'of first
rate stars. FRITZ Massary remains the
queen Of the Teuton soubrettes despite
the fact that her success was won a
score Of years ago. Claire Dux, one
time grand opera favorite, and Vera
Schwarts, also of Berlin's State opera.
both were weaned from the classical
stage last year and will help some in
getting the popular Vienna works over
this difficulty. but there are not enough
winsome and talented singers, and this
gives the managers great anxiety.


Richard Strauss, composer of "Sa-
lome." is reported to have invaded the
operetta field with a work to be per-
formed this fall at the Metropole The
atre with FRITZ Massary and her hus-
band. Max Pallenberg. Germany's best
known comedian. in the stellar roles.
Strauss wrote the libretto himself. and
Ia said to have succeeded with naive
but amusing domestic subject.

The natives of St Kilda. in the Heb
rides. have decided to abandon a quaint
custom which they have followed for
more than a century. of electing their
own queen. Hereafter they will take
the natural descendant. They have de-
posed Queen Margot and will recognize
Mary as their sovereign


This news comes here as the first
communication from the Island since
last September and was brought to Lon
don by a vessel which delivered census
papers at the island this week. The
natives there speak only Gaelic. but the
census papers were printed In English.
Otherwise the chief happenings on the
island include an Influenza epidemic,
which caused many deaths.


Persons aboard the ship who could
converse with the natives said the chief
question on the island was whether the
war had broken out again. .

Officials Of the Pacific Mail Steam
ship Company yesterday confirmed the
report from San Francisco that the
company is planning fortnightly pas
senEer and freight service from New
York in January. In addition to
strengthening the water route for
freight traffic between the two coasts
the company states that this will give
New Yor the only direct passenger line
with San Francisco and California.


The first sailing will be that of the
Venezuela from San Francisco on Jan
uary 8. Her pioneer voyage west
bound will start from New York on
February 8. She will be joined later by
her sister ships, the Ecuador and Co
lombia, and by the Santa Ana. The first
three liners were built in 1915 express
ly for service in warm climates and
until recently were maintaining the
Pacific Mails "Sunshine Belt to the
Orient" The Santa Ana was built in
1917 for service through the Panama
Canal to the west coast Of South Amer
ica.


The inauguration of the new line is
the first passenger and freight service
Of the Pacific Mail since the days of
transshipment at Panama. The COM
pany dispatched its first steamer from
New York for the gold fields of Caifor-
MIA in 1848. When the company was
incorporated in that year for the car
riage of United States mails to the
scattered settlements on the Pacific
Coast the American clipper ships were
dominating the ocean. Ir the three
quarters Of a century since that time
the Pacific Mail has been operating
continuously under the American flag
In more recent years it has extended
its services to the Far East


The first passengers which the COM
pany carried from the Atlantic sea-
board in more than half century were
on the Shipping Board passenger and
cargo liner Creole State, assigned to
the company for operation in its Ma
nilaEast India route. She was loaded
in Baltimore year ago for her voy-
age to the home port of San Francisco.

But the traces Of their civilization are all dis
tinctly Monaghan, while those that came after,
and over them, resemble Egyptian.


The ashes and charcoal that lie just above
give meditative dggers ground for believing
that whoever they were who once inhabited
this high mountain-circled valley volcano
ended them.


Was it Popocatepetl, which to-day sends up
ominous clouds of smoke, or ''The Sleeping
Woman" who still sleeps? Who knows?


In the soil that then gradually settled over
these ashes and these buried people are now
found skulls, but no body skeletons, and
pieces Of pottery badly broken and not to be
matched. It is thought that blood wiped out
these, and that then came period when man
no longer lived here, while great animals
roamed at their ease among dense and luxu-
rious vegetation. For here are huge deer horns,
and elk, and javeln teeth.


For man came again-great migratory
tribes from the north. The animals were
driven out, the rank vegetation subdued.
These new people built cement floors to their
houses-and laid streets.


These were the last people to sink into the
soil Of Mexico. Here, only about three feet
from the surface, lies the remains of the ad-
vanced Aztec civilization.


Here is decorative pottery Of high class.
Here are clever tools, finely made from bone,
needles for sewing, needles for knitting,
spindle whrls similar to those found in Troy,
cylinders for rolling manuscript, tools for
printing, pipes for high glaze.


It is clearly established that these people
were the Aztec who founded the city Of
Mexico-that they called Tenochitlan-in the
early part Of the fourteenth century.


But who those were who went before them.
no one can say, although the Aztecs have a
vague myth of great fire and great deluge,
and two great peoples destruction.

Up In the woods and fields of Maine

SYRIAN, Samara Province, Sept. %
(By MaiD There are no boating songs
on the Volga his year.


The balalaika is not ringing from
the few boats which are floating along
this once mighty river whose sholow
waters are affording a poor avenue of
escape from the parched grain fields,
which mock the peasants to whom they
formerly yielded abundant bread. Pawn
brokers have long since received the
Dalalaikas in exchange for rubles nee
essary to buy food for the starving fam
lilies.


Samavors no longer sing merrily on
the hearths of the peasants cottages.
They too have been exchanged for
bread. Together with the family ikons
and the bright brass cendlesticks that
once adorned every mantelpiece, they
are exhibited in the secondhand shops
former owners are huddled together
in miserable camps along railways and
rivers waiting for somebody to take
them to land of food,


Priest who are as miserable as
their parishioners have set UP affairs
in the wayside camps and are burying
the dead and praying for the half
dead, who kneel submissively before
the cross and intone their petitions to
heaven at sunrise and sunset.


Fortunately, the sun does not fail
them often. The autumn has been dry
so far and the glorious Indian summer
has made their lot less intolerable than
it will be when autumn rains add to
the misery of the unsheltered, poorly
clothed, hundreds of thousands.


A few families are still floating down
the river in frail rowboats, stacked
high with children and battered house
hold utensils. The conditions are about
as bad Gown the Volga as they are
here, but the more restless refugees
say they feel better to keep moving
Some families still have horse or an OK
which has managed to live on parched
stubble and are dragging along behind
their rickety wagons until the time
dead.


Cemeteries surrounding the quaint
churches. which line the entire course
of the Volga, are crowded with ref
ugees.


But there is no shower of mama.
The drought and the grasshoppers
have robbed them Of bread. Their
prayers have been of little avail
Their priests have not been able to get
them food. Their Little Father. who
formerly looked after them in famine
times, is no more. Yet they have not
utterly. lost hope and still devoutly
cross themselves and feebly voice petit
tlons, as they slowly merge into the
dust to which they are so soon to
return.

PARIS, Nov. 8 (By Mail) Black re-
mains supreme in the fashion world Of
Paris. Despite severe onslaught by
advocates of color, the supreme council
of style has been forced to retain the
conventional black as the dominant
motif of all fall and winter modes. and
there is every indication that colors,
except IN minor trimming effects, will
not be able to challenge black until
late spring.


Adopted at a time when economy was
the. guiding idea Of all feminine pur-
.hases, black has come to be regarded
as the most becoming color. French
women say it is alone in lending itself
to striking effects.


Dressmakers quietly gathered to-
gether before fall and winter models
were given to the world and tacitly
agreed that colors should have
chance The adoption of black was
hurting them financially. Done black
of two or three dresses Of different
colors.


Women Reply Emphatically "No"


But the French women who are in
dicators of the newest DEVELOPMENTS
in style, said very emphatic "No!"
The demand this fall was for black





inevitable. Crepe Moroccan, velvetine
and perlIaine arc the most popular
materials.


The corset makers. however, have
been slightly more successful in their
efforts to bring the corset. back into
it's own. Dressmakers are insisting
that corsets arc now necessary to give
the "uncorseted look This propa-
ganda has succeeded in some instances,
but most French women, having fought
and won their freedom, are loath. in
actress, ito Jail their bodies again.


There arc four definite features Of
the fall and winter modes: Il very long
waist line, longer circular skirts with
full sides. eccentric sleeves of gay COT
ors and the famous Bateau neck line.


Brick red has been used extensively
as trimming and some green steel orna-
ments for hats, purses, dresses and
even shoes arc the newest thing in noy-
elites.


Kniekerbocker" Shoes Poplar


Door knobs and nailhead effects are
used in making girdles. In the case of
shoes, the usual order Of things has
been reversed and the smarest shoes
in Paris are "knickerbocker" shoes,
with large steel buckles.


These shoes look more like American
shoes than anything ever before worn
by French women, although the French
last is retained. The short, stuhby toe
has disappeared in stylish French foot
wear.


Black again dominates in hats, felt
being the best liked material. Crowns
are much higher, and the fall hats are
so big that they interfere with dancing.
Smaller hats will be worn with fur
coats later in the season.


Circular earrings, usually circle of
jet rebonv within larger circle, are
worn by the NEST dressed women this
fall Novelty shops cannot make them
fast enough. Some women wear very
large ones, almost cannibalistic in
effect


Gay cyolor has its only opportunity
in evening gowns for young girls.
These are made in the brightest of
cclors, but the evening dresses worn by
their mothers and older relatives are
black. The Empire period has given
the inspiration for the youthful even
ing dresses this year, making wearers
look like venerated ancestors. The
skirts are large and full, with hips ex-
tended.

Flames shooting Off the roof Of the
nineteen story Vanderbilt Hotel at
Park avenue and Thirty fourth street,
provided thriller for thousands in
the streets soon after 10 o'clock last
night A combination paint and print
ing shop 80 to 20 feet encased in gal
vanized iron, was ripped apart by an
explosion of painting materials and
caught fire People in the streets heard
the explosion and glanced upward, 10
see a rolling cloud of smoke drift over

fourth street side. A moment later the
heavy smoke was split by bright
flames.


Firemen under Acting Chief Martin
quickly arrived at the Thirty-fourth
street side and carried coils OF hose
into elevators and were shot up to the
roof BY that time the engines were
ready to keep the water pressure In the
stand pipe to the roof The burning
shop was toward the Thirty-fourth
street side. and some Of the water let
loose on it went over the edge, spraying
the crowd in the street.


The burning materials included heavy
paper stocks. on which the hotel print
ing was done, and the painters sup
plies. In the shop were two printing
presses. which were damaged, the
total loss being about $4,000.


While the firemen were working the
police reserves cleared the streets for
two blocks each side OF the hotel. The
flames were quickly subdued, but the
smoke kept pouring off the roof for
some time. There was little excitement
in the hotel. even with a fire engine
pumping outside. Many of the guests
never knew that anything had hap
pened. But some were nervous and
sent down inquiries. and even decided
10 stand down in the lobby for awhile.
despite assurances that there was posi-
lively no danger. as the Vanderbilt was
fireproof To the last word.


Half an hours work finished the fire.
smoke and all. and the excitement died
down The flames had been visible
south to Fourteenth street and north
to Fifty-frst street and west to the
Hudson River. Acting Chief Martin said
the explosion and fire were due to
spontaneous combustion.

BOSTON, Feb. 12.-The rescue at sea
of the thirty-six men comprising the
crew OF the Belgian freighter Bombar-
dier as their ship was going down was
described to-day when they arrived here
on the succoring steamship Mount Clay.
The latter. bound from Hamburg for
New York, but diverted to this port.
formerly was the German commerce
raider Prinz Eitel Friedrich.


With their decks awash and heavy
seas crashing upon them, the men of
the Bombardier lost two of their four
lifeboats when they tried to leave the
ship Wednesday morning. Then Chief
officer Outeway managed to put off with
ten men In safety, and sixteen men got
away in another boat Meantime the
Mount Clay had put over a lifeboat for
rescue work and picked off ten men who
remained among them Capt. Mathes OF
the Bombardier, who was last TO leave
his ship She sank soon afterward, the
crew believes.


Tho Bombardier, formerly operated by
the Shipping Board as the Iris. was car
rying general cargo from New York
for Antwerp when she encountered a
hurricane Monday and sprung leak.
Buffeted by the storm, the seams opened
and water flooded coal bunkers and en-
gine room, extinguishing fires, putting
radio apparatus out Of commission and
washing coal into the pumps, which be-
came clogged. The wireless was restored
sufficiently to send out feeble distress
signals that called the Mount Clay, fifty
miles away.
